少女をとめ革命かくめいウテナ 鳳雛子 作

An alternate history in eighteen parts

Utena, 1885: the Meiji serial and the world it made

What if all thirty-nine episodes of Revolutionary Girl Utena had first appeared as a pseudonymous illustrated serial in a Tokyo newspaper in 1885, four years before Japan wrote its constitution and thirteen before it wrote its family law? This is the history of that serial, from its first installment to 2026.

Written October 2026. Real history is marked documented; what follows from it, inference; where I picked one outcome among several, choice.

I

The premise and the rules of the game

What appears, where, and what is held fixed

On Thursday, 2 April 1885, Jiyū no Tomoshibi (自由燈, "The Lamp of Liberty"), a Tokyo "small newspaper" of the kind that printed its kanji with readings beside them so that shop clerks and their wives could follow, carried the first installment of a new serial novel. Its heading read 少女をとめ革命かくめいウテナ, Otome Kakumei Utena, and under it, where an author's name would go, stood three characters nobody recognised: 鳳雛子.

Over the next two years, in four parts and thirty-nine chapters, interrupted twice by the police and finished in book form, that serial told the whole story of the 1997 television series Revolutionary Girl Utena: Utena Tenjō in her boy's jacket, Anthy Himemiya and the duels for the Rose Bride, the Student Council and its creed of the chick and the egg, the Black Rose, Akio Ōtori and the night rides, the Rose Gate, and Anthy walking out of the academy at the end. This document works out what follows. Where the record allows, it uses documented history. Where the record runs out, it reasons from the nearest documented case and says so.

The idea comes from a forum thread that asked what the classical world would have made of Tolkien's legendarium if it had been found in antiquity, and from an earlier companion piece that sent the first Magic: The Gathering cards back to 1593. That piece transported the cards unchanged. A television series cannot travel that way. Thirty-nine half-hours of animation, with their sports car and planetarium and electric lift, would be magic in any century before the twentieth, and magic is the wrong genre for this story. So the first rule here is different.

The rules of the thought experiment

A novel, not a relic. What appears in 1885 is a work of fiction written in 1885, by someone living then, in the language, print technology and visual conventions of a Tokyo newspaper of that year. Nothing comes from the future, and nobody in this history ever learns that the story existed anywhere else. The premise is simply that this book was written. The question of where its author got the story does not arise, any more than it arises for Genji.

The story intact. Every episode has a chapter, in order. The events, the people, their names and their relations are the series'; so is everything the series refuses to explain (what Akio shows his passengers, who lit the fire at Nemuro Memorial Hall, what happens to Utena). What changes is the furniture. Where the anime uses a machine or a custom 1885 did not have, the serial uses the nearest thing an 1885 reader could picture, and one that carries the same charge where possible: Akio's sports car becomes a light carriage he drives himself, the planetarium becomes an orrery and a magic lantern, blood types become the family register. Part IV gives all thirty-nine chapters side by side with the episodes.

An author nobody can name. The byline is a pen name and stays one. I do not decide who wrote the serial. Part XIV sets out what the scholars of this timeline argue, and leaves it there.

Everything else is real. Laws, prices, people, newspapers, wars and institutions behave as the record says they behaved until the serial gives them a reason to behave otherwise. When I say that something happened differently, I say why, and what in the record makes it plausible.

Real people. Real people appear in this history, because a story that mattered in Meiji Japan would have mattered to them. What they do differently is labelled, and kept to things their own records make likely. I never put invented words in a real person's mouth. The quoted letters, notices and reviews in Part XVI are by invented people.

Impact is allowed. A cultural object cannot rewrite a constitution by itself. It can tip decisions that were already close, give a movement a vocabulary, a set of symbols and an audience, and change what a generation takes for granted. When it does, I follow the consequences forward, through law and money as well as literature, and do not stop at listing what might have changed.

How to read the labels

Three labels run through the whole document. documented marks real history, sourced in Part XVIII. inference marks what follows from documented conditions once the serial exists: a prediction, argued, that a reader could dispute. choice marks a place where several outcomes were plausible and I picked one; those are the places to push back. A sentence with no label is either the serial's own content (which is the anime's) or connective tissue. The buttons in the contents rail highlight any one kind.

What this document is not

It is not a novel, and it is not a summary of the anime. It is a systematic working-out of one premise: the serial itself (Parts III and IV); how its first readers read it (V); a chronicle from 1885 to 2026 in five parts (VI to XI), with a detour abroad (VIII); its economy (XII); what it did not change (XIII); the authorship question (XIV); its texts and editions (XV); a set of period documents (XVI); and the two timelines side by side (XVII).

The short version

For readers who want the outcome before the argument, these are the largest differences between this timeline and ours, each argued in the Part named:

  • A newspaper enriched and a word coined. The serial swells the sale of a hounded Liberal paper until the Asahi buys it, gives schoolgirls words for their attachments a generation early, and makes the rose the flower of love between women (Parts VI, VII, XII).
  • The throne closed a little more firmly. The imperial household's draft allowing female-line succession is killed in 1886 as in our history, with one more argument against it (Part VI).
  • Women on the stage sooner. An all-woman Utena at the Misaki-za in 1893; a Takarazuka Utena in 1919; a film actress in 1918 (Parts VII, IX).
  • The vote that passed. The House of Peers passes women's local suffrage in 1931 and frees wives from legal incapacity sixteen years early (Part IX).
  • A classic in every classroom. From 1952 every senior high school student reads its first and last chapters (Part X).
  • Two roads abroad. A French Fiancée des roses read in the Paris salons, and a Chinese 少女革命 read by the women students of Tokyo (Part VIII).
  • Today. More women in the Diet, a partnership law for same-sex couples, and the same first woman prime minister (Part XI).

And much does not change at all: the wars, the empire, the mills, the household law of 1898 and the governing party (Part XIII).

A note on names. Japanese names are given family name first when they are real people of the period (Kishida Toshiko, Tsubouchi Shōyō) and in the anime's familiar Western order when they are the serial's characters (Utena Tenjō, Akio Ōtori), as English writing about both usually does. Long vowels are marked (Ōtori, Tōga) in running prose; the anime's English spellings ("Ohtori", "Touga") appear only where they are the series' own.

II

Why 1885

The earliest year the story can be told whole, and the last in which it can still change the laws

1885 is the first year in which every piece of Utena's furniture exists in Japan or in Japanese print, and the year before the state began, law by law, to fix the shape of the modern Japanese family. A story about breaking the shell of the world lands while the shell is still being made.

Japanese names and a Japanese setting were a preference of the request, and they rule out most of the world. Within Japan I weighed six moments. The table compares them on the five things the premise needs: a medium that can carry thirty-nine episodes with pictures; a world that can hold the series' Western furniture without magic; names that read naturally; a censor strong enough to make the book dangerous but not strong enough to erase it; and decisions still ahead of it that a book could tip.

MomentMediumThe Western furnitureThe censorWhat lies ahead

Genroku Osaka, c. 1700Illustrated prose fiction or a puppet playOnly as the exotic of the Dutch trading postLight, sporadicToo far from the modern questions the story asks

An earlier sketch of this premise set the story in Tenpō Edo, as a gōkan. The medium fits beautifully: the gōkan was the most picture-led serial form in the world before the twentieth century, illustrated on every page, with characters drawn in the likeness of kabuki actors, the nearest thing pre-modern Japan had to an animated cast. documented But the story's furniture is Western, and the Edo telling would have had to invent a European academy, a European prince, a European witch and a rose garden out of nothing. In Meiji Japan those things were arriving by the shipload, and the Edo version would have spent its energy explaining what 1885 could simply show. inference

The medium threshold

By 1885 Tokyo had two kinds of newspaper. The "large papers" (ōshinbun) were written in dense literary Japanese for officials and political men. The "small papers" (koshinbun) printed every character with its reading beside it, ran crime, scandal and theatre news, and from the late 1870s carried tsuzukimono, serial stories in daily installments, each with a woodblock illustration. documented The small papers were read aloud in households, barbershops and bathhouses, so their audience was larger than their circulation and included many people, women above all, who could not read a large paper. documented (Part XVIII)

A daily installment with one picture is the closest thing to an animated episode that 1885 possessed. Every morning a reader got a scene, a cut and a cliffhanger, and a serial's chapter of five to eight installments ran about a week, the same rhythm as a weekly television episode. Serials were then reissued as illustrated volumes and, if they were popular, staged. documented A girl who reads Utena in 1885 hears it read aloud at breakfast, buys the picture of the duel as a single sheet, sees the women's troupe play it at a Yokohama theatre, and reads it again in a book. That is the life of a television series, rebuilt from what 1885 actually had. inference

The Western threshold

Every piece of the anime's furniture has an 1885 equivalent that a reader had seen or read about:

  • The academy: the mission schools on Yokohama's Bluff, Ferris above all, founded in 1870 and on the Bluff since 1875, with Western buildings, dormitories, pianos and English teachers; the Peeresses' School opened in Tokyo that year. documented
  • The ball: the Rokumeikan, the government's hall for Western-style balls, open since November 1883. documented
  • The duels: Western fencing taught to army officers; Japanese swordsmanship in police training and public exhibitions after the 1876 ban on wearing swords, a ban on wearing them, not on owning them; young women with halberds fought in the first public sword shows of 1873, and in the 1880s, by the usual account, the dormitory mistress of the peers' daughters was Chiba Sana, a licensed swordswoman. documented
  • The car: the private carriages of ministers and peers, the most visible luxury in Tokyo; there were some 1,800 passenger carriages in the whole country in 1885. documented
  • The lift, the phonograph, the telephone: a freight hoist at a Tokyo paper mill since 1875, and a mine-shaft cage in the Iwakura Mission's published record; a phonograph demonstrated in Tokyo in 1878 and shown to the public in 1879; about two hundred telephones in government offices and none in private hands. documented
  • The planetarium: the orrery, which is what English called a "planetarium" until the projector was invented in the 1920s, and the magic lantern, which the Ministry of Education had been sending to normal schools since 1880 with sets of astronomical slides, and which one of its photographers had been showing free to Tokyo crowds since 1883. documented
  • The roses, the prince, the witch, Lucifer: Western roses in Yokohama gardens; Aesop in a new Meiji translation in the 1870s (the Jesuits had printed one in 1593) and the Arabian Nights in Japanese since 1875, the first books of Grimm from 1887; the New Testament complete in Japanese in 1880. documented

None of this was ordinary. All of it was known, which is what a fantasy needs: the reader must be able to picture the conservatory, the carriage and the lift without ever having been inside one. inference

The legal hinge

Between 1884 and 1900 Japan wrote down, for the first time, who a woman was in law. In 1884 it created a modern peerage, with princes. In 1889 the Imperial House Law restricted the throne to men, the first such rule in Japanese history, which had had eight reigning empresses. In 1890 a law on assemblies barred women from political meetings and associations, and the Imperial Rescript on Education set out the family morality every school would recite. A fight over the Civil Code from 1889 to 1892 ended with the liberal draft shelved, and the code of 1898 made the household head the master of the family and the wife a legal incompetent. In 1899 the state organised girls' secondary schools around the ideal of the "good wife and wise mother", and in 1900 it reaffirmed the ban on women in politics. documented (dates in Parts VI and VII)

A serial that began in 1885 and finished in 1887 reached its readers before every one of these decisions. A girl of fourteen who cried at chapter 39 in 1887 was twenty-five when the family law of 1898 came into force. That is the leverage the premise needs. Earlier, the furniture is missing; later, the law is written. inference

The censor

The press law of the 1880s let the Home Ministry suspend a newspaper or seize an issue for disturbing public order or public morals, and it did so constantly; editors went to prison by the dozen. Books had to be submitted before publication. In December 1887 a new ordinance expelled some 570 activists from the capital within three days. documented (Part XVIII) That is enough to make Utena dangerous, to cut it and to stop its serialization, and not enough to destroy it. Meiji Japan banned many books; it did not have the means or the will to pulp a best-seller that had already been printed in tens of thousands of copies. inference

The reach

The 1880s and 1890s were the high point of Western Japonisme. Japanese prints filled Paris, Japanese plays toured Europe and America by 1900, and a Japanese book with pictures could cross into French or English within a decade. From the 1880s Korean and from 1896 Chinese students came to Tokyo to study modern ideas, men first and women in the 1900s and 1910s, and they read what Tokyo read. documented A serial of 1885 has both routes open, and Part VIII follows them.

What 1885 costs the scenario

Honesty requires the downsides. In 1885 about a third of Japanese girls of school age were enrolled in elementary school, and the Ministry of Education counted nine girls' secondary schools in the whole country, with 616 pupils; the new Peeresses' School had 133. documented There was no "girls' market" for publishers to sell to; Utena has to build one. The small newspapers' buyers were mostly men, and the serial's first audience is a household's, read aloud by a father or an elder brother. The paper that runs it is a party organ without a party, in political trouble from the start. The story's third part, with a grown man's courtship of a schoolgirl and an incestuous brother, is more dangerous in 1886 than in 1997, not less. Each of these is a friction, and each, worked through, produces history rather than preventing it.

III

The serial

What appeared, where, when, in what form, and under what name

Otome Kakumei Utena ran in a Liberal party paper that changed its name while the serial was in it, was suspended by the police two chapters before the end of its third part and given up when that part ended, and was finished as a book. The newspaper it began in became, in 1888, the Tokyo Asahi.

The paper

Jiyū no Tomoshibi, "The Lamp of Liberty", was founded on 11 May 1884 by Hoshi Tōru as the popular organ of the Liberal Party, the Jiyūtō: a small newspaper, in the small papers' style, meant to carry the party's ideas to readers who would never open its serious daily. documented Five months later the party dissolved itself, on 29 October 1884, under police pressure and the shame of the risings its radicals had led. documented The paper survived it. On 14 January 1886 it renamed itself Tomoshibi Shinbun, on 1 April 1887 Mezamashi Shinbun ("Wake Up!"), and on 10 July 1888, bought by the Osaka publisher of the Asahi, it reappeared as the Tokyo Asahi Shinbun, the paper that would later employ Natsume Sōseki and, in 1940, merge with its Osaka parent into the national Asahi. documented

It was not a struggling paper. For a time in 1884–86 it had the largest sale in Tokyo, and part of the reason was fiction. documented From December 1884 it had been serialising Miyazaki Muryū's Kishūshū (鬼啾啾, "Ghosts Wailing"), a history of the Russian nihilists whose heroines were Vera Zasulich, who shot the governor of St Petersburg, and Sophia Perovskaya, hanged for the assassination of Alexander II, who in Muryū's telling gives up the man she loves for "ten million compatriots". The serial ended on 3 April 1885; its book edition was banned in October and Muryū was convicted. documented Political fiction had been allegorising Japan's politics as a woman courted by rival suitors since 1880, when the first political novel cast the people's rights as a geisha named O-Ken ("Rights") wooed by "People" and "Government". documented The paper's readers were therefore primed for exactly what arrived in its mailbox in February 1885: a story with "revolution" in its title, a girl who fights in a man's coat, and a bride whom rival suitors win by force. inference It also needed a successor to Kishūshū. inference

The first installment

It appeared on Thursday 2 April 1885, the day before the last installment of Kishūshū, under a two-line heading beside the day's woodblock cut. choice The opening is the anime's fairy-tale prologue, told in the voice of an Edo storyteller, with the narrator's doubt at the end turned into the kind of aside a gesaku author made to the reader. The mock-up below sets the opening as the paper would have printed it, in vertical columns read from right to left, with the readings beside the harder characters. The Japanese is new writing for this document, in the literary style of 1885, and is not a translation of the anime's script.

The shape of the serial

The newspaper printed about 210 installments in a year and a half, and the unserialised Part Four was the length of about forty more. A chapter took between three installments (the "story so far" chapters) and nine (chapter 39), usually five to seven, so a chapter took about a week of reading, much like a weekly episode. Each installment had one cut. Each chapter ended with a notice naming the next chapter's heading and the same unexplained tag, 絶対運命黙示録. choice for the counts.

The pictures

The cuts were signed 芳年: Tsukioka Yoshitoshi, the greatest print artist of the day, who had begun a series called One Hundred Aspects of the Moon that very year and who had got into trouble in 1884 with another Liberal paper for supplying pictures to Jiyū no Tomoshibi. documented for Yoshitoshi's 1884 work for the paper and his newspaper illustration in general; choice that he drew this serial. The plates of the 1887 book were by his pupil Mizuno Toshikata. choice Each newspaper cut was a small woodblock, cut by a professional carver from the artist's drawing and printed with the text: line only, no tone, no colour. documented for the method. Within those limits the illustrator invented most of what later generations thought of as the look of Utena, because the text describes very little: Utena's long hair loose under a boy's cap, which she never wears in the anime and always carries in the cuts; Anthy's spectacles as two blank white circles; the duelling garden as a flat ellipse seen from an angle, with the upside-down castle cut off by the top of the frame; the silhouetted girls of the shadow plays against a wall of rose lattice. The single-sheet colour prints that publishers made from the most popular scenes added the colours readers argued about for decades: a pink that 1880s aniline dyes made almost violet for Utena's hair, a deep red-brown for Anthy's skin, black for Akio's carriage. choice

The language

The narrative is in the mixed literary style of 1885, Edo storyteller's rhythms over a frame of Sino-Japanese, with a narrator who steps forward now and then to address the reader. The dialogue is in the spoken Tokyo Japanese of its speakers, which is how the small papers already wrote dialogue and how the serial gets most of its effects. documented for the convention. Each character's speech places them in 1885 society as exactly as their clothes:

  • Utena says 僕 (boku) for "I" and 君 (kimi) for "you", the pronouns of male students. In the anime she uses the same boku; in 1885, from a girl, it is a social act, and the first thing readers imitated. inference
  • Anthy speaks the soft, deferential language of a maid in a great house, calls Utena ウテナ様, and changes the form of address with each new owner, exactly as in the anime. To readers who had been in service, that was the most frightening thing in the book.
  • Nanami and the Kiryū household speak the new Yamanote dialect of rich Tokyo families, with its -asobase and its onii-sama; Saionji the clipped orders of a swordsman; Akio the easy, self-mocking courtesy of a man educated abroad.
  • The narrator calls himself, or herself, "the author" (作者) and never says which.

The readings beside the words

Small papers printed the reading of every character, and the serial uses the space beside the text to play. Its most famous glosses became part of the language:

少女 → をとめ
The title's "girl", read otome, the older word for a maiden (Part XV).
決闘者 → デユエリスト
"Duellist", glossed with the English word in katakana, as political novels glossed liberty. The duel itself was news: 決闘 in the sense of a formal, pre-arranged fight was first debated in Japanese in 1881, glossed with the native word for a samurai's settled combat. documented
世界の果て
"End of the World", left unglossed throughout, so that readers could not be sure even how to say it. choice It is the serial's central mystery, and Part V lists the guesses.
牛鈴 → カウベル
"Cowbell", in chapter 16: a cow's bell, glossed as an English brand-name might be.
鳳学園 → おほとりがくゑん
"Ōtori Academy". Schools of 1885 were 学校, 女学校, 塾 or, for the mission schools, 学院; the compound 学園, "school-garden", has no dictionary example in our history before 1906. documented In this timeline the serial coins it, for a school that is mostly a garden, and it is the word every private school founded after 1890 wants in its name. choice
総代会 → そうだいくわい
"The Council". There were no student councils in Japanese schools before the Occupation, and the word 生徒会 is a post-war one. documented The serial uses 総代, the word for the pupil chosen to speak for a class at a ceremony, and makes a council of them. choice The nearest real thing was at the Meiji Girls' School, founded that year, whose pupils came to sit on its governing council and to run their own dormitory. documented The chairman of the board is the 校主, the proprietor, as private schools then called their owners, and Akio is his 代理; "chairman of the board of directors" would not be Japanese for another twelve years. documented for the dates of the words.
王子 → わうじ
"Prince". Meiji Japanese had no settled word for the prince of a fairy tale: a crown prince was 皇太子, an emperor's grandson 皇孫, and 王子 was the son of a foreign king. When Tsubouchi Shōyō retold Cinderella for a school reader in 1900, her prince became a 若殿, a young lord. documented To a Tokyo reader Ōji was also a village north of the city, with a famous fox shrine and the paper mill whose freight hoist, installed in 1875, was Japan's first lift. documented The serial's prince is therefore foreign by definition, and a little bit of a fox.
男装 → だんさう
"Men's dress", of a woman, in chapter 1. The dictionary's earliest example of the word is from a novel of 1889. documented Here it is four years older, and it is the serial's word for Utena's whole manner, not only her clothes. choice
永遠 → えいゑん
"Eternity". A new word: the philosophers' dictionary of 1881 had fixed it as the translation of the English eternity. Ordinary people said 永久 or とこしへ. documented The castle that holds "eternity" therefore sounds, in 1885, like something out of a lecture on Western philosophy, which is exactly the effect. inference
魔女 → ウヰツチ
"Witch", in chapter 34. Read in the ordinary way, the characters meant manyo, a she-demon of Buddhist scripture; the European witch did not yet have a Japanese word. documented The serial glosses it with the English word, so that the Rose Bride is accused in a foreign language. choice
彼の女 → かのをんな
"She", in the heading of chapter 31, in the older spelling; the newer 彼女, read かのぢよ, was just entering print.

The book editions

The paper reissued each part as soon as it finished, in three illustrated paper-covered volumes per part with colour-printed covers, in the format the old Edo picture-serials had used and that Meiji publishers still used for newspaper fiction. documented for the practice. Part Four appeared first as a typeset book in April 1887, published by Shun'yōdō, the house founded in 1878 that would later publish most of Ozaki Kōyō and Natsume Sōseki, and that had reissued a Liberal newspaper serial, Sakazaki Shiran's life of Sakamoto Ryōma, as a book in 1885 (documented for the firm; choice that it published this book), and all thirty-nine chapters were collected in four volumes in 1888. The textual history of those editions, which is more interesting than it sounds, is in Part XV.

IV

The thirty-nine chapters

A concordance: each episode of 1997 beside the chapter of 1885–87 that tells the same story

Every episode of the television series has a chapter in the serial, in the same order, with the same events, the same people under the same names, and the same things left unexplained. The serial's author changed the furniture and nothing else.

The table gives each chapter's heading as it stood in the newspaper or the 1887 book, in the serial's literary Japanese, with a reading and a translation; then the episode it matches; then what the 1885 telling does with it. Two habits run through it. Where the anime used a machine that 1885 did not have, the serial substitutes the nearest thing an 1885 Tokyo reader could picture and, if possible, one that carries the same charge: an adult's carriage for an adult's sports car, a magic lantern for a planetarium projector, a family register for a blood-type chart. And where the anime's Japanese title rests on a pun, the serial finds a Meiji pun to put in its place. choice All headings are my compositions; their spelling follows the mixed habits of the 1880s press, with historical kana in the readings. So is everything the third column and the notes below say about the serial's reception: reprints, readers' names and reactions, the censor's marks. choice

The part titles are the newspaper's (第一編 to 第四編). The names in brackets are the ones readers gave them, and which stuck: the third part has been "the Carriage Book" since 1886, much as the anime's staff called their third arc the sports-car arc.

No.The serial's headingWhat the 1885 chapter does with the episode
Part One 第一編 [the Council Book, 総代会の巻] · chapters 1–13 · Jiyū no Tomoshibi, April–August 1885
1薔薇の花嫁Bara no hanayomeThe Rose Brideep. 1 · The Rose BrideOpens on a boxed "Western tale" printed in a ruled frame like a page of an imported picture book: an orphaned princess, a travelling prince on a white horse, a ring, and the narrator's gesaku aside that resolving to become a prince herself may not have been wise. Ōtori Academy stands on a bluff above a harbour in Kanagawa; its woman teacher objects to Utena's boys' high-collared jacket and red knee breeches, and Utena answers that no rule forbids them. She beats the boys' baseball nine single-handed. The birdcage conservatory is iron and glass, like the palm houses in imported prints. Wakaba's letter is pinned on the notice board; the challenge comes in the kenjutsu hall; the gate in the forbidden wood opens when water falls on her ring; the stone stair climbs to the duelling garden under a castle hanging upside down, which Saionji calls a mirage (蜃気楼). He draws the sword from Anthy's breast; Utena fights with a bamboo shinai cut short and wins with the stub. Anthy is waiting at the gate: she belongs to Utena now.
2誰が為に薔薇は微笑むTa ga tame ni bara wa hohoemuFor Whom the Rose Smilesep. 2The council rides a hydraulic lift up the tower. No reader had ridden one: Japan's only lift was a freight hoist at a paper mill, and the nearest thing in print was Kume Kunitake's account of the Iwakura Mission, whose envoys were hauled up a mine shaft near Newcastle in an iron cage and felt "as if rising from the underworld to heaven". On the way up the council recites the creed of the chick and the egg, printed in the clipped Sino-Japanese of a proclamation. The empty east dormitory; Anthy's tea; Chu-Chu, "a small beast of the southern seas, neither mouse nor monkey". Saionji's exchange diary becomes an exchange notebook of letters. Utena means to lose, shields her rose by reflex, and a young man in white with a red-lined cape dives from the castle into her. The illustration of the dive was reprinted as a single-sheet print within the month.
3舞踏会の夜Butōkai no yoruThe Night of the Ballep. 3 · On the Night of the BallA ball at the Kiryū mansion in the manner of the Rokumeikan, which had opened eighteen months earlier: bustled gowns, a naval band, dance cards. Tōga shows Utena a ring like hers. Nanami sends Anthy a gown that a "waiter" ruins with champagne; Utena comes down the stair in her own jacket, crosses the buffet, makes a gown of a tablecloth and dances with Anthy, and Chu-Chu cues the band. The first chapter to be read as satire of the Rokumeikan.
4光さす庭　序の曲Hikari sasu niwa: jo no kyokuThe Sunlit Garden: Preludeep. 4Miki Kaoru, piano prodigy, tutors Anthy and hears in her playing the sound he lost as a child. Nanami's three "Operations" (snail, snake, octopus) are each undone by what Anthy keeps in her pencil box, drawer and cupboard; the snake meets a mongoose, a creature most readers knew only from Indian travel books. Anthy serves sweetened ice for dinner, crushed with a mallet in the manner of the ice-water shop Yokohama had had since 1869.
5光さす庭　終の曲Hikari sasu niwa: tsui no kyokuThe Sunlit Garden: Finaleep. 5The twins' story: the day Miki had measles and his sister went on stage alone. Kozue leaves the music room straightening her dress; Tōga is inside. Miki duels with his own fencing foil, evenly, until Anthy calls out for Utena. Measles was no metaphor to the 1885 reader; most families had lost a child to it.
6七実様御用心Nanami-sama goyōjinTake Care, Miss Nanamiep. 6The first comic chapter, in the old gesaku manner. Runaway horse, the boy Tsuwabuki and his embroidered handkerchief, the bull he once watched Tōga stop. Nanami records his confession on a phonograph (the 蘇言機, "machine that brings words back to life", first demonstrated in Tokyo in 1878), and the chapter's climax is a boxing kangaroo escaped from a travelling circus, felled by Tōga in Western boxing drawers.
7見果てぬ樹璃Mihatenu JuriJuri Unfulfilledep. 7 · Unfulfilled JuryArisugawa Juri, captain of the academy's French fencing, duels to prove that miracles do not happen. Shiori and the stolen boy are told in tableaux; the string telephone is a children's toy of the day. The locket holds a carte-de-visite photograph cut from a class picture, and the last line shows whose face it is. The sword falls from the air and spears Juri's orange rose; Utena never touches it. The chapter that made the serial notorious.
8華麗なる天竺道中Karei naru Tenjiku dōchūThe Splendid Road to Indiaep. 8 · Curried High TripThe anime's pun on 華麗 (splendid) and curry survives, because one Meiji spelling of curry was カレイ: the heading's ruby gives both. A cooking-class curry explodes and swaps Utena's and Anthy's minds; Nanami is packed off to India by mail steamer for the spice; every glimpse of India ends in elephants, and she comes back sunburnt. Saionji's notebook, Chu-Chu's banana, and the discovery that the explosion was simply Anthy's cooking.
9永遠ありといふ城Eien ari to iu shiroThe Castle Said to Hold Eternityep. 9The two boys share a hired tricycle in the rain, the toy every Tokyo boy wanted in the early 1880s, and enter a church with three coffins laid flat in the Western way, which to a reader used to seated barrel coffins was itself uncanny. A girl lies among roses and wants to be left there. Anthy is taken; the word the serial uses is the anime's own, kamikakushi, spirited away, which in 1885 still described something that happened to children. Tōga takes the cut meant for Utena's back.
10七実の大切なるものNanami no taisetsu naru monoNanami's Precious Thingep. 10Tōga's birthday party, a Western custom then practised only by the most Westernized families, since everyone else grew a year older at New Year. Nanami's sabre and dagger. Her memory: a taped box at the edge of a sluice. Readers who had heard Kishida Toshiko speak in 1883 on "daughters in boxes" made the connection at once.
11優雅にして冷酷　其の花を摘む者Yūga ni shite reikoku: sono hana wo tsumu monoGraceful and Cruel: The One Who Plucks That Flowerep. 11Tōga watches the picnic through opera glasses, claims to be Utena's prince, and wins when she falters. Anthy leaves on his arm and starts calling her "Miss Tenjō". The serial's readers had now watched a woman pass from one owner to a third, and the letters column filled.
12或は友情の為にAruiwa yūjō no tame niPerhaps for Friendshipep. 12 · For Friendship, PerhapsUtena comes to school in the girls' uniform, which in 1885 means a Western day-dress of the kind the girls' normal schools were about to adopt. Wakaba shames her into taking herself back. She fights Tōga in the dress with a borrowed foil, and the shaft of light that Anthy makes of the Sword of Dios shreds it. "Let's just go home."
13描かるる軌跡Egakaruru kisekiA Locus Tracedep. 13 · Tracing a PathThe serial's first "story so far", the convention by which newspapers re-told a long serial for new subscribers. A man whose face is never drawn reviews the duels for a silent prince seated on a sphere; each duel bears a plaque with a French word (アミチエ, amitié, with a kanji gloss), the language of Meiji law and the army. A phonograph cylinder repeats the creed. Last images: a glowing jar, a pinned butterfly, a black rose.
Part Two 第二編 [the Black Rose Book, 黒薔薇の巻] · chapters 14–24 · Jiyū no Tomoshibi, renamed Tomoshibi Shinbun on 14 January 1886 · October 1885–February 1886
14黒薔薇の少年等Kurobara no shōnen-raThe Boys of the Black Roseep. 14Akio Ōtori appears: acting chairman, betrothed to the chairman's daughter Kanae. To an 1885 reader the different surnames of Anthy Himemiya and her brother explain themselves: he has been taken into the Ōtori house as adopted heir and son-in-law to be, the commonest arrangement in Meiji family law. His tower room holds an orrery and a magic lantern that throws the stars on the dome. Under Nemuro Memorial Hall, Mikage interviews the troubled in a descending lift whose framed specimen regresses from butterfly to leaf. White lilies on the desks: the Easter lily, which Yokohama nurseries were beginning to ship to America.
15其の梢の指す景色Sono kozue no sasu keshikiThe Landscape the Treetop Points Toep. 15 · The Landscape Framed by KozueKozue, who drives off everyone near her twin. The milkshakes become iced drinks, a foreigners' treat in Yokohama since 1869, which Kozue refuses from Miki's hand and, after the duel, asks him to make again. Akio gives Utena a magic-lantern slide of the moon: a brother is something useless you look up at now and then. The council's creed is heard once with "cage" in place of "shell".
16幸福の牛鈴Kōfuku no kauberuThe Cowbell of Happinessep. 16The shopping channel becomes a newspaper advertisement in English for "Bullock & Co., Jewellers", which Nanami cannot read. She wears the bell with every outfit and turns, by degrees, into a cow, an animal Tokyo had only lately learned to eat. Anthy knits a red shawl. Utena plays matador. The bell was for Anthy's own cow, also called Nanami.
17死の棘Shi no togeThe Thorns of Deathep. 17Shiori comes back, finds the locket, learns whose face it holds, and draws Juri's sword from Juri's breast. Christian readers heard the heading as the "sting of death" of First Corinthians, the phrase the 1880 New Testament had just put into Japanese.
18美蔓もどかしMitsuru modokashiMitsuru Impatientep. 18 · Mitsuru's ImpatienceThe boy who wants to be grown up at once studies kissing, for which the translated fiction of that very year was making 接吻 the standard word, in a translated English novel of the kind that had been a runaway success in 1878–79, instead of the anime's films. Mari's bitten bar of chocolate was a confectioner's novelty in Tokyo. He cuts Utena's hair: a woman's cropped hair had been a fineable offence in Tokyo from May 1872 until the Penal Code of 1882, and in 1886 it still made people turn in the street.
19今は亡き王国の歌Ima wa naki ōkoku no utaSong of a Kingdom Now Lostep. 19 · A Song for a Kingdom Now LostTatsuya, Wakaba's "Onion Prince", is turned away from the Mikage lift for being a good person. The onion was a Western vegetable newly grown in Hokkaido, which made the childhood taunt a joke about a girl's hairstyle. Saionji is in Wakaba's room.
20若葉繁れるWakaba shigereruWakaba Flourishingep. 20Saionji carves Wakaba a leaf-shaped hairpin, a kanzashi rather than a clip; it ends gilded in Anthy's hair. "I'm a face in the crowd." Utena will not draw on a friend, takes Wakaba's own sword from her, and cuts the rose.
21悪しき虫Ashiki mushiVerminep. 21Keiko lends Tōga her umbrella, a Western "bat umbrella" and a status object in its own right, and is cast out by Nanami. Akio teaches Utena the Pleiades, which every reader knew as Subaru, and Castor and Pollux, which few did.
22根室記念館Nemuro kinenkanNemuro Memorial Hallep. 22Professor Nemuro, a prodigy no older than the hundred boys he leads toward "eternity"; Tokiko, the woman inspector sent by the board; her dying brother Mamiya; the fire. The serial says only "long ago", and readers placed it where 1885 kept its own dead boys: the Aizu youths of 1868 and the Kagoshima academy students of 1877. Nobody is shown lighting the fire.
23決闘者の資格Duelist no shikakuThe Terms of a Duelistep. 23The heading glosses 決闘者 with the English loanword デユエリスト, a trick the political novels used for liberty and revolution. Utena challenges Mikage. Akio ends him by telephone, an instrument a few ministries had and no school did: "graduate from this place." The hall is a ruin; Miki cannot remember its name; "Mamiya" was Anthy.
24七実様内証日記Nanami-sama naishō nikkiMiss Nanami's Secret Diaryep. 24 · The Secret Nanami DiaryThe second "story so far", done as Tsuwabuki's pocket diary read aloud at his bedside, with Nanami, Utena and Anthy drawn as shadows on the bed-curtain. Like the anime, it re-tells only the comic chapters, since the Black Rose duellists remember nothing.
Part Three 第三編 [the Carriage Book, 馬車の巻] · chapters 25–33 · Tomoshibi Shinbun, May–October 1886; suspended for nineteen days after chapter 31, and given up after chapter 33
25二人の永遠黙示録Futari no eien mokushirokuThe Eternal Apocalypse of the Twoep. 25 · Their Eternal ApocalypseThe girls move into the tower. Akio explains his name: the morning star, Lucifer, who chose to be king of hell; 黙示録 was the new Bible's word for Revelation. Then the ride. Tōga cups his ear for the sound that races through the End of the World, and the sound is hooves and iron tyres: Akio's light open carriage, crest on the door, which he drives himself at night along roads lit by gas lamps. There were fewer than two thousand passenger carriages in all Japan, and a minister's had a coachman on the box: Ōkubo Toshimichi's had died defending him in 1878. Akio drives his own, and readers took the detail as the measure of the man. At the moment the anime has him vault onto the bonnet, he stands up on the box and lets the reins fall, and the horses run with nobody driving. In the duel, overturned carriages stand on the garden floor with their lamps throwing beams upward, and the Sword of Dios thins to nothing. Anthy draws a new sword out of Utena.
26幹の巣箱　光さす庭 替手Miki no subako: hikari sasu niwa, kaeteMiki's Nest Box: The Sunlit Garden, Alternate Partep. 26The anime's "Arranged" becomes kaete, the shamisen term for a second part played against the first. Miki's father remarries, and the faceless bride on the telephone wears the Rose Bride's gown. Kozue waits at night for her "patron", a word that in 1886 meant what it means in the licensed quarters, where the anime has her "Daddy Long Legs" (a book not yet written). She rides on the box beside Akio; Miki sits alone behind.
27七実の卵Nanami no tamagoNanami's Eggep. 27Nanami wakes beside an egg and decides she laid it. Juri's line about "my balls" survives because she bowls; Japan's first bowling alley had opened in Nagasaki's foreign settlement in 1861. Tōga's verdict on girls who lay eggs; Saionji frying eggs in an apron; Chu-Chu home in a jacket and tie.
28闇に囁くYami ni sasayakuWhispers in the Darkep. 28Ruka comes back to the fencing club after a long illness that the chapter never names; readers of 1886, who lost so many young people to consumption, named it for themselves. Shiori and the sword she says she polished; the carriage; the duel; "I failed because of my bride."
29空より淡き瑠璃色のSora yori awaki ruri-iro noAzure Paler than the Skyep. 29Juri's duel; the locket broken in the rain. The shadow-play slot before the duel holds only Shiori, standing before the rose wall; the shadow play proper comes after it, two nurses gossiping in a hospital corridor about a patient who died yesterday. Trained nursing was the newest profession open to women in Japan (the first schools opened in 1885–86), so the scene was also news.
30跣足の少女Hadashi no otomeThe Barefoot Girlep. 30A Western cake and three candles in a branched candlestick; two go out. Akio kneels and takes off Utena's buttoned boot, the footwear of a schoolgirl who has given up clogs, and kisses her beside the carriage. Later he takes off his fiancée's mother's shoe in the same way: "My only prince." Tōga holds up the other boot and asks after the owner of the glass slipper.
31彼の女の悲劇Kano onna no higekiHer Tragedyep. 31The heading writes "her" as 彼の女, read かのをんな, the older of the two ways the translators of the day rendered the Western she; the newer 彼女, read かのぢよ, was just entering fiction. Nanami's discovery comes from the family register, where the anime has blood types (discovered in 1901): what the register shows her about her brother and herself is not what she expected, though the chapter never prints it. Lost at night in the tower, she comes round the back of the sofa, and the chapter ends on what she saw, which it never names.
32踊る女等の恋Odoru onna-ra no koiThe Romance of the Dancing Girlsep. 32Nanami cannot say what she saw. Kanae sits slack on the sofa while unseen hands feed her slices of apple, a scene that 1886 read through the "poison-woman" stories its papers had sold since Takahashi Oden's trial. Tōga draws a single sabre from her; she loses on her feet.
33夜を走る王子Yoru wo hashiru ōjiThe Prince Who Runs Through the Nightep. 33The radio quiz becomes the prize-riddle column of a newspaper inside the novel, kept by two girls, and Akio writes in under the pen name 世界の果て and answers neither riddle. Which is eternal: a diamond, a beautiful memory, or tinned peaches? Which is a miracle: Edison's inventions, meeting a prince, or a tinned mermaid? Utena spends the evening at an inn on the Sumida on the night of the river fireworks, talking to someone who is never drawn. The Reversi game becomes go, and the proverb she half-says is 待った無し, no taking moves back. In the newspaper the chapter's last illustration was a blank frame, captioned "this picture withheld."
Part Four 第四編 [the Apocalypse Book, 黙示録の巻] · chapters 34–39 · published as a book only, Shun'yōdō, April 1887
34薔薇の刻印Bara no kokuinThe Rose Crestep. 34The shadow girls step out from behind their wall as the Kashira Shadow Players and stage The Tale of the Rose in silhouette before Utena, Anthy and Akio. Then the memory: the barn, the prince in the straw, a telegraph key clattering on its own, and outside a mob of faceless men in Western suits with sabres demanding he save their daughters. "Dios is no longer here!" The million swords.
35冬のころ芽生えし愛Fuyu no koro mebaeshi aiThe Love That Blossomed in Wintertimeep. 35Akio courts Utena on a white horse, the mount of the princes in the new foreign picture books and, in the oldest Japanese verses about a prince on horseback, of the young Buddha riding out of his father's palace; the censor's copy of the book marks the passage, which tells us what the censor thought a white horse meant. Tōga delivers earrings, a foreign ornament, since Japanese women did not pierce their ears. The poppy maze, in the decade when Japan's papers were full of opium in China.
36斯くて夜の扉開くKakute yoru no tobira hirakuAnd Thus Opens the Door of Nightep. 36The carriage ride parodied on a two-seated "sociable" tricycle, Tōga pedalling and Saionji standing up in his seat to declare it time to rise from their coffins. Tōga's confession; the last council duel. That night Utena crosses the tower room and finds Anthy with Akio.
37世界を革命する者Sekai wo kakumei suru monoThe One to Revolutionize the Worldep. 37Utena takes off the ring. Tea and talk of cantarella, the Borgias' poison; "in ten years we'll have tea and laugh like this." Anthy goes off the edge of a roof cornice and Utena catches her cuff. The ring is back on; the letter is taped together.
38世界の果てSekai no hateEnd of the Worldep. 38Akio in a prince's white uniform; Utena put in a pink gown and crown. Then the reveal, which 1887 understood instantly because every reader had been to a lantern show: the castle is a slide in Akio's magic lantern, thrown on the dome of his room, and there is no higher place. The duel; "I'm going to be a prince!"; the blade from behind.
39何時か共に輝かんItsuka tomo ni kagayakanSomeday, Together, We'll Shineep. 39 · And Someday, Together, We'll ShineThe Rose Gate; the million swords that shine with human hatred; Utena's bloody fingers at the seam; the coffin; fingertips. Utena vanishes from the academy's world. The school forgets her within a season. Anthy leaves her spectacles on Akio's desk and walks out through the gate in a pink travelling suit, with a trunk and Chu-Chu, down a road over green hills. The book's last plate is a photograph in a rose-coloured mount, with a third figure cut off by its edge.

The recurring machinery

The anime's set pieces have to survive as print, and they do, in forms the Meiji press already had.

The storybook prologue
A boxed "Western tale" opening chapters 1, 3, 8, 13, 16 and 31, set in a heavier rule like the imported picture books sold at Maruzen. The prince's face is never drawn.
The creed
Printed in proclamation style, unattributed, whenever the council rides the lift. From 1886 it was the most quoted passage in Japanese.
The shadow plays
Two girls drawn as black silhouettes against a rose-patterned wall, in the convention of kage-e shadow prints, trading a riddle or a skit before each duel. Each opens with a short formula that readers chanted; the serial gives the girls no names.
The duel songs
Each duel installment prints a chorus in the new-style verse of the 1882 Shintaishi-shō, packed with the vocabulary of the decade's science (evolution, embryology, the galvanic cell) wound round Buddhist terms. They were set to music by the 1890s, and the stage versions sang them.
The descent
In Part One the figure who dives from the castle is drawn whole only twice, in chapters 2 and 11, as in the anime's first arc; later chapters give him a line of text and, in the cuts, a small diving shape, as the anime gives him a few frames.
The previews
Each chapter ends with a 次回 notice naming the next heading and closing on the same cryptic tag, 絶対運命黙示録, "Absolute Destiny: Apocalypse". Nobody in the serial explains it.
The recaps
Chapters 13, 24 and 33 are the serial's three "story so far" chapters, placed where a newspaper needed them, at the end of a part.
V

How 1885 read it

Seven readings, all of them partly right

Meiji readers were trained to look through a story for the thing it was really about. The Edo habit of reading comic fiction and prints as coded comment on the authorities, and the 1880s fashion for political novels set in Greece or Ireland that were obviously about Japan, made every serious reader a decoder. documented Utena gave them almost too much to decode.

1. A political novel in disguise

The paper's own readers, Liberal men who had lost their party in October 1884, watched the Chichibu rising crushed a few days later, and spent the winter reading about Sophia Perovskaya in the same column, read it first as a political novel. documented for the dissolution and Chichibu. The creed of the chick that must break the world's shell read like a handbill. The Student Council, sons and daughters of rich houses who rule the academy from a balcony in the sky and take their orders from sealed letters signed "End of the World", read like the oligarchs of Satsuma and Chōshū and their circle, who governed by rescript from behind a screen. The Rose Bride, who belongs to whoever wins her by the sword, was "the people's rights": prized, fought over, and never consulted, like the geisha O-Ken ("Rights") of the first political novel, courted in 1880 by "People" and "Government". documented for the 1880 novel. Utena, the commoner in borrowed clothes who fights for the Bride and is not a prince, was the movement itself. inference The police read that way too. When Kishida Toshiko spoke on "daughters in boxes" at Ōtsu in October 1883, the inspector's report took the box for the government's press and assembly laws, the parents for the government, the daughter for the people, and the servants sent after a daughter who elopes for the police in the hall. documented Anyone who could decode a speech about daughters could decode a novel about a bride.

The names helped. Saionji, the hot-tempered vice-president who strikes the Bride and wants to possess her, shares a surname with Saionji Kinmochi, the young noble back from Paris whom an imperial order had forced out of a liberal newspaper in 1881. Arisugawa, the cool fencer who duels to disprove miracles, shares a name with an imperial prince's house. documented for the real Saionji and Arisugawa. Readers could take the borrowings as satire, as homage or as carelessness, and argued about which. inference When the Osaka Incident broke in November 1885 (Liberal activists arrested for a plot to start a revolution in Korea, with a twenty-year-old former schoolmistress, Kageyama Hideko, among them), the papers that disliked the Liberals had their headline ready: the Liberals' girl revolutionaries were no longer only in their fiction. Kageyama had, by her own account, cropped her hair and dressed entirely as a boy until she was sixteen, while the local children jeered at her as a "fake", and she had carried the plotters' explosive chemicals in a trunk because nobody searched a woman's luggage. documented for the Osaka Incident, Kageyama's arrest and her own account; choice for the headline.

2. A book about marriage

Women heard it differently, often aloud, often in the evening, at an age when few of them could read the paper themselves. inference To them the Rose Bride was not an abstraction. A Meiji bride was chosen by her parents through a go-between, transferred with her goods to her husband's household, entered in its register, and expected to obey its head; that is what "engagement" meant, and the serial's word for Anthy's state, 婚約, is the ordinary one. documented for the marriage customs. Anthy, who is engaged to whoever holds the sword, calls each new owner by a new form of address and smiles, is the most exact portrait of a Meiji wife in Meiji fiction, and she is drawn as a horror. inference

The rest of the household is drawn as exactly. Akio's position, which a modern viewer must puzzle out, needed no explanation in 1885: a young man of no family betrothed to the chairman's daughter and taken into the house as adopted heir, ruling it while the old man is ill, and the reason the siblings Himemiya and Ōtori have different surnames. The adopted son-in-law was a commonplace of the Meiji family, and so was his reputation for owing everything to his wife's house and resenting it. documented for the institution. Mrs Ōtori, who calls her daughter's fiancé "my only prince" in chapter 30, was the mother-in-law of a hundred kabuki plays turned inside out. inference And the boxes and coffins that run through the serial (the coffin girl in chapter 9, the taped box at the sluice in chapter 10, Mikage's drawers dropping into the fire) arrived eighteen months after Kishida Toshiko had told an audience in Ōtsu that Japanese parents kept their daughters like goods "in boxes", and been arrested for it. documented for the speech and arrest. No woman reader in 1885 needed the connection made. inference

3. A schoolgirls' book

The girls of the mission schools on the Bluff read it as a book about themselves, and they were the first to read it in packs. They lived in dormitories, played the piano, learned English and French, had senior girls they worshipped, and were watched for signs of corruption by a press that had decided "schoolgirl" meant trouble. documented for the mission-school milieu and the press's attitude. In Utena they found a school that was theirs made strange and grand, a heroine who answered back to teachers, and a world in which the important relationships were between girls. inference Within a year they were exchanging carte-de-visite photographs in lockets (a practice Meiji schoolgirls already had), giving each other white roses, and calling each other by the serial's forms of address; within two, the word Bride had become the dormitory word for a younger girl attached to an older one, and prince for the older. choice In our history the schoolgirls had no name for these attachments until the slang o-me was reported in 1909 and esu ("S", for "sister") spread in the 1910s; the clinical 同性愛 came later still. documented In this timeline the words come a generation early, out of a novel, and carry its romance and its menace together. inference Part VII follows what became of this.

4. A Christian book

Japan's Christians in the mid-1880s numbered a few tens of thousands: about 30,000 Catholics in 1884, a Protestant membership that was growing fast after the revival of 1883, and the Russian Orthodox converts besides. documented They were a small community but a disproportionately literate, urban and female one, concentrated around the very schools where the serial was most read. inference Christian readers recognised what others missed. Akio introduces himself as Lucifer, the morning star who chose to rule in hell. The last arc's word for revelation is the new Bible's. The heroine's prince is called Dios, the Spanish for God. No Japanese text of the period uses that form, but Catholic readers heard in it でうす, Deusu, the sixteenth-century word for God that the French missionaries' catechisms of 1868–72 still printed as a gloss, and that their hidden-Christian grandparents had prayed to in secret. documented for the catechisms. And the Rose Bride, pierced by a million swords for the sins of others and unable to die, comes out of a devotion the French priests had brought with them: Our Lady of Sorrows, whose soul, in Simeon's prophecy in Luke, a sword would pierce. documented for the devotion and the verse, which the New Testament of 1880 had put into Japanese; whether any Japanese church had an image of her with swords is not known. The missionaries were divided. Some preached against the serial's incest and its girls' love; some of their Japanese teachers, women above all, read it as a parable of the soul held captive by the world and of the one who reaches into the coffin to save it. inference

5. An allegory of the throne

The most dangerous reading took longer to form, and the government was quicker to see it than most readers were. The castle that hangs over the duelling garden is "the castle said to hold eternity". Japanese political rhetoric of the 1880s already described the imperial line as unbroken for ages eternal, and in 1889 the constitution would put the phrase in its first article. documented A castle said to hold eternity, a prince on a white horse whom everyone worships and who turns out to have fallen, a man who rules from a tower by projecting the castle onto the sky with a lantern, and a girl who is told that she cannot be the prince because she is a girl: by 1889, each of these had a meaning in Tokyo that the author of 1885 may or may not have intended. inference The parallel with Princess Kazu was easier still. Engaged as a girl to Prince Arisugawa Taruhito, she had been given instead to the shogun Iemochi in 1862 to bind the court to the shogunate, a Rose Bride transferred from one champion to another for reasons of state, and she had died only in 1877. documented Older readers who remembered her journey to Edo did not need to be told why a girl called Arisugawa stood on the council. inference Anthy's own surname made it worse. 姫宮, himemiya, is the word The Tale of Genji uses for an imperial princess, and in the 1880s, when each child born to the emperor was given a personal title ending in -miya, a commoner girl called Himemiya sounded at best presumptuous. documented for the word and the custom. A princess of the blood, kept in a tower, engaged to whoever wins her: the censors' copy of the 1887 book marks the surname every time it appears. choice

6. A comic novel with a modern heart

The literary men read it as a gesaku, the comic popular fiction of Edo that the new criticism was trying to bury, and were unsettled to find it moving. Tsubouchi Shōyō was publishing The Essence of the Novel in parts from September 1885, arguing that the novel's subject was human feeling, shown truthfully, not moral lessons or marvels. documented In this timeline the treatise never mentions the serial, but the younger critics who took up its terms applied them to it at once, as a case of feeling truly observed inside a frame of marvels, and regretted the marvels. choice The verdict stuck to the book for a generation: true in its people, false in its castles. It took the critics of the 1920s to argue that the castles were the truth, and the people's feelings the projection. inference

7. A scandal

The police and the moralists read it as a list of offences. A girl in a man's coat: Tokyo's minor-offences ordinance had punished "women who dress as men" from August 1873, with exemptions for actors and for women in hakama, and in April 1881 the Yomiuri had reported a crop-haired fishmonger's daughter in Shiba, in a workman's coat and tight trousers, being summoned and "admonished" under it, after which she eloped with a girl from a tea stall at the Shiba Shinmei shrine. The reporter found a woman falling for a woman "too strange". documented The ordinance had lapsed when the new Penal Code took effect on 1 January 1882, and the Penal Code had dropped the clause; whether Kanagawa's police rules kept one is not known. documented So Utena broke no law that anyone could name, which annoyed the moralists more. Girls who love girls. A brother and sister. A grown man, engaged to be married, who courts a schoolgirl, and his fiancée's mother besides. Schools where boys and girls are taught together, which the Education Order of 1879 had forbidden above the elementary level. documented And the word revolution in the title, in the paper of a party that had just been dissolved. The surprise is not that the serial was suspended in 1886 but that it ran for nearly seventeen months before it was. The answer, in this timeline, is that the Home Ministry was watching the paper's politics, not its fiction, and by the time the fiction was the reason it sold, closing the best-selling paper in Tokyo had become costly. inference

Who was who

By the end of 1886 the guessing game had settled into a set of identifications that every reader knew and no editor would print. Akio was Itō Hirobumi, prime minister from December 1885, whose charm and appetite for women were common talk. documented for Itō's reputation; choice for the identification. Nemuro's hundred boys were the boys of Aizu who died on Iimori Hill in 1868, or the students of Saigō Takamori's academies who followed him to death in 1877; readers chose by region. documented for both events; choice for the readings. End of the World was the oligarchy, or the emperor, or the West, or simply adulthood, which is the reading the anime's own writer arrived at a century later. choice for the readers; documented (makers' statement: Enokido Yōji, 1998) for the writer's. Nobody identified Utena. She was, as the girls of the Bluff said, whoever was reading.

Her name did its own work. うてな was a word every reader knew from Buddhist sermons and the theatre: the lotus seat of those reborn in paradise, the seat that the lovers of The Tale of Genji vow to share, and so, through the puppet plays of Chikamatsu, the "one lotus" (一蓮托生) that lovers hope to share by dying together. documented for the senses of the word. A heroine called "the lotus seat" who ends the book reaching for another girl's hand across a coffin lid was read in 1887, by everyone who knew their Chikamatsu, as a love-suicide refused, or postponed. The book does not say which, and the argument has never stopped. inference Older readers had a word for what she was, too: 変成男子, henjō nanshi, the Lotus Sutra's dragon king's daughter who becomes a man in an instant so that she can become a buddha, a phrase Edo comic verse had used since at least 1753 for a woman in men's clothes. documented In the serial's first year the word came back into the street as the name for a girl who dressed like Utena. choice

Shadow play · Part V

ADo you know, do you know? In 1885 a whole city read one story and each reader found a different book in it.

BThe Liberals found a pamphlet. The wives found a marriage. The Christians found a saint. The police found a charge sheet.

AAnd the schoolgirls?

BThe schoolgirls found each other.

VI

Chronicle, 1885–1890

The serial years, and the six years in which Japan wrote down what a woman was

For five years Utena was news. It ran, it was stopped, it was staged, it was argued about in the letters columns and the lecture halls, and it gave a generation of girls a way of speaking, dressing and pairing off that their elders could see and could not stop. Its first effect on the law was the opposite of what its readers hoped.

Each year below threads the serial through documented events. Entries marked documented happened on those dates in our history; the threads are marked inference or choice.

1885The Council Book

Winter. The Matsukata deflation is at its worst; rice is cheap, farmers are selling land to pay taxes, and the Chichibu rebels of the autumn before are being tried. The Liberal Party has been dissolved since October. documented In February the first three chapters of a serial arrive at Jiyū no Tomoshibi by post. choice

2 April. Chapter 1 appears. It takes over the space left by Miyazaki Muryū's nihilist serial, which ends the next day, and for a month it is one entertainment among several in a paper that already has one of the largest sales in Tokyo. documented for Kishūshū and the paper's standing; choice for the rest. The first sign of something else comes from Yokohama, where the paper is sold at the station and in the foreign settlement's Japanese shops: the agent there orders more copies every week from mid-April, and by May the paper's Yokohama sale has trebled. The mission schools on the Bluff are reading it. choice

18 April. Itō Hirobumi and Li Hongzhang sign the Tianjin Convention, withdrawing both countries' troops from Korea. documented

May. Chapter 7, Juri's chapter, ends with the photograph in the locket. The letters column, which normally prints three or four letters a week, prints eleven, most of them from women, and the paper runs a second column of letters for the first time in its history. choice Some are outraged; more are grateful; one, signed "a woman of Kōjimachi, aged forty", says only that she had a friend like Shiori once and had not thought of her for twenty years. choice This is the moment when the serial stops being a political novel in disguise and becomes the thing its readers will remember: the first story in modern Japanese print in which a girl's love for a girl is the point of a chapter, stated in a picture and left without comment. inference

4–12 June. Fukuzawa Yukichi's editorials "On Japanese Women" run in his Jiji shinpō, with a continuation in July: Japanese men should imagine their positions and their wives' reversed, and a society that expects women to bear what men could not is not civilised. documented Tokyo's most influential liberal and its most popular serial are arguing about the same thing in the same weeks, and readers notice. Fukuzawa never mentions the serial; its letters column mentions him often. choice

June. The serial pauses for two weeks while the paper waits for manuscript. On 19 June a schoolgirl's letter points out that the byline can be read as a girl's name (Part XVI, document 2). choice

Summer. Girls on the Bluff begin to wear black boys' jackets over their kimono and hakama on the walk to school. In Tokyo the first are seen in Kanda, near the private schools, by August. choice Girls in men's clothes had drawn official notice once already: in 1872 the government's first girls' school had put its pupils in samurai men's hakama, and the same spring Tokyo forbade women to crop their hair, on the ground that it blurred the line between men and women. documented The jackets reopened the question in a new form. Shops near the schools start selling "ウテナ形", Utena-style jackets cut for girls, and a Yokohama ring-maker sells cheap brass rings stamped with a rose for 5 sen, a day's pocket money. choice The girls' new habit of saying boku draws the letters that document 3 imitates. choice

20 July. Jogaku zasshi, the "Magazine of Women's Learning", begins publication in Tokyo. documented Its Christian editors will spend the next five years arguing with Utena without ever naming it in print. choice

21 August. Part One ends with chapter 13, the "story so far". The paper announces a second part for the autumn and the first three volumes of the book edition. choice By then its daily sale is half as large again as it was in March, and the paper is the best-selling in Tokyo by a distance. choice (Part XII gives the numbers.)

September. Tsubouchi Shōyō begins publishing The Essence of the Novel, in nine parts that will run to April 1886. documented

13 October. Part Two begins, and with it Akio. The same month Tōkai Sanshi's Chance Encounters with Beautiful Women appears. documented for Kajin no kigū; choice for the serial's date. For the rest of the decade students will argue about which of the two heroines, the Irish revolutionary Kōren or Utena Tenjō, a young man should prefer, and the girls of the Bluff will settle it for themselves. choice

November. A women's theatre company plays The Rose Bride of the Bluff at a small Yokohama house (document 4). It is the first of hundreds of unauthorised stage versions, and the first time a Japanese audience sees a woman play a girl who plays a prince. choice On 23 November police in Osaka and Nagasaki arrest dozens of former Liberals for a plot to send explosives to Korea and start a revolution there; among them is a twenty-year-old former schoolmistress, Kageyama Hideko. documented She idolised Joan of Arc, and historians would call her the Joan of Arc of the East. documented In this timeline the papers, which have all read their rival's serial, call her "the Utena of Osaka". choice The Home Ministry suspends Jiyū no Tomoshibi for ten days in December, nominally for its reporting of the arrests. choice The serial misses a week.

22 December. The cabinet system replaces the old council of state; Itō Hirobumi becomes Japan's first prime minister and Mori Arinori its minister of education. documented

1886The Black Rose and the Carriage

14 January. Jiyū no Tomoshibi becomes Tomoshibi Shinbun. documented The serial's chapter 21 runs in the last issue under the old name and chapter 21's second installment in the first under the new; readers say the paper changed its name and the serial did not notice. choice

February. Part Two reaches Nemuro Memorial Hall. The fire, the hundred boys and the professor who calls their deaths a necessary sacrifice arrive in a city where most adults remember the boys of Aizu on Iimori Hill and many families had sons at Saigō's academies in 1877. documented for both. Letters come from Aizu and from Kagoshima, each claiming the hundred boys for its own dead. The serial never says. choice

March–April. Mori's school ordinances reorganise Japanese education from the Imperial University down to the elementary schools, and make normal schools into barracks of discipline. documented The model of schooling the serial mocks (a school that trains its pupils to be pieces in a game run by an absent authority) becomes official policy the same spring. Mori himself, who had once published an argument for monogamy and married by written contract, is the cabinet's leading advocate of women's education, and the oligarchs' least predictable reader. documented for Mori's views; choice for his reading. In this timeline he reads the serial, and while he lives his ministry, alone among the government's, never moves against it. choice

Spring. The rose fever begins. Western roses had come in with the treaty ports, and the first Japanese manuals on growing them, translated from American books, had appeared in 1875; but the rose was still a collector's plant. Tokyo knew what a craze could do. In 1872–73 imported rabbits had changed hands for fifty, a hundred and once six hundred yen, until on 7 December 1873 Tokyo prefecture taxed every rabbit a yen a month and within days a kit sold for two sen; and from about 1877 to 1885 the potted omoto had its own boom of books and prices. documented In the spring of 1886 the rose becomes a speculation in its turn. White roses sold as "Utena" change hands for a yen a plant; a dark red-violet sold as the "Bride" goes for five, then fifteen; nurseries in Yokohama and Komagome import French stock by the crate. choice Part XII follows the bubble to its crash.

1886. A sixteen-year-old samurai's daughter from Sendai, whose father had named her Tarita, "enough girls already", runs away to join a touring troupe of sword-fighters, who bill her as "the beautiful swordswoman"; as Sonobe Hideo she will become the greatest woman fighter of the age, and in 1899, before an imperial prince, she is said to have made a famous swordsman of sixty-one abandon a bout against her. documented In this timeline the troupe's posters that year show her in a black jacket. choice

11 May. Part Three begins, the Carriage Book. Within a month the press attaches Akio's name to every young man with a private carriage, and a fashion for driving oneself at night spreads among the sons of the rich, whom the police of Tokyo had never had to regulate before. choice

14–16 June. More than a hundred women of the Amemiya silk mill in Kōfu walk out against new guild rules that lengthen their day from fourteen hours to fourteen and a half and forbid them to move to another mill, shut themselves in a temple, and win a relaxation of the rules in two days: the first factory strike in Japan. documented Nothing connects them with the serial. Most of the strikers could not read, the paper did not circulate in Kōfu, and the story's academy is the opposite of their dormitories. inference Their strike is a reminder of how narrow the serial's world was: it was read in schools, shops and houses with a newspaper subscription, not in the mills, which employed more women than all the schools in Japan.

Summer. Cholera kills more than a hundred thousand people across Japan. documented The serial's readers, like everyone else, are frightened; the letters column shrinks.

21–22 August. Chapter 31 ends with Nanami behind the sofa. The Home Ministry orders the issue seized and the paper suspended for "injury to public morals" (documents 5 and 6). choice The suspension lasts nineteen days. When the paper returns, chapters 32 and 33 appear with passages blanked; on 19 October the last cut of chapter 33 is printed as an empty frame and the serial editor announces that the story will be finished as a book. choice

24 October. The British freighter Normanton sinks off Wakayama; its British officers take to the boats and leave all twenty-five Japanese passengers to drown, and a British consular inquiry at Kobe acquits the captain; after a public outcry he is tried at Yokohama in December and given three months, and the drowned passengers' families receive nothing. documented The fury over extraterritoriality fills the papers for months and buries the serial's suspension as news. inference

December. Yajima Kajiko, the first head of a Tokyo mission girls' school, founds the Tokyo Women's Reform Society, the Japanese branch of the Woman's Christian Temperance Union, with herself as president. documented Its founders disapprove of the serial. Many of its younger members have read it twice. choice

1887The Apocalypse Book

January. The empress, who had first appeared in Western dress the previous summer at the Peeresses' School, issues a memorandum urging women to adopt it: the kimono of the day, it says, is a bad legacy of the age of civil wars, and Western dress, divided into upper and lower garments, is closer to the dress of ancient Japanese women. documented The girls who have been wearing a boy's jacket since 1885 take it as permission. choice

1 April. Tomoshibi Shinbun becomes Mezamashi Shinbun. documented The same month, Part Four appears as a book, after the Home Ministry's censor has removed one passage about the white horse (Part XV). choice It sells its first printing of 10,000 copies in nine days. choice Readers who had waited six months for the end got the Rose Gate, the coffin, the fingertips, Utena's disappearance and Anthy walking out of the academy gate in a pink travelling suit. The ending's force in 1887 is hard to recover. In a society where a woman left her father's house for her husband's and her husband's only for the grave, a young woman walking out of her brother's house alone, with a trunk and no destination, to look for someone she loves, was not a romance. It was a scandal and a promise. inference

20 April. Prime Minister Itō gives a fancy-dress ball at his official residence, and a scandal about the prime minister and a nobleman's wife follows it. The paper that had serialised Utena, renamed Mezamashi three weeks before, reports the scandal and is suspended for eight weeks; in all it spends 133 days of 1887 under suspension. documented (Part XVIII) Readers who had finished Part Four the week before needed nobody to tell them what Akio Ōtori was. The identification of Akio with Itō, which had been a joke, becomes a political weapon, and Liberal speakers begin quoting the serial's carriage-ride line, "I will show you the End of the World", in the halls where they attack the government's foreign policy. choice

Summer. Foreign Minister Inoue Kaoru's treaty-revision talks collapse under public anger at their concessions; he resigns in September, and the Rokumeikan era ends with him. documented The book of the ballroom, as some critics called Utena, outlives the ballroom. inference

1887. Roses bloom in the titles of popular fiction: a storyteller's "European novel" called The Yellow Rose, and Cherry and Rose, The Rose in Two Colours and In the Shadow of the Rose, all published that year. documented In this timeline every one of them is sold as being "in the manner of Utena". choice

Autumn. The first kabuki Utena, an authorised adaptation by the house playwright of the Shintomi-za, opens to full houses: a girl playing a prince, played by a man who specialises in women, which kabuki audiences found more natural than the women's companies did. choice Its most admired scene is the ball. Its most cut scene is the last.

25 December. The Peace Preservation Ordinance takes effect the day it is issued, and between the night of the 26th and the 28th some 570 activists are ordered to leave Tokyo, by the rule that bars anyone the police think dangerous from living within three ri of the palace. documented Among them is the paper's founder, Hoshi Tōru; without him Mezamashi falls into a crisis that ends with its sale to the Osaka Asahi. documented Among them too is the Liberal politician Nakajima Nobuyuki, and his wife, who appears on it as Nakajima Shōen: Kishida Toshiko. He goes to Yokohama and she follows; in March 1888 they settle in Ōta, on the western side of Yokohama, and in May she becomes an honorary professor at Ferris. documented In this timeline the expulsion list also includes the paper's former serial editor. choice The Nakajimas' move to the city of the Bluff, and Kishida's chair at the school every reader thought the academy was modelled on, are the foundation of the Kishida hypothesis about the authorship (Part XIV). inference

1888The collected edition and the crash

Spring. The rose bubble bursts. A dealer in Komagome who cannot pay for forty crates of French roses kills himself, the papers discover that the "Black Rose" plants sold for thirty yen were ordinary crimson roses grown in shade, and prices fall by nine-tenths in a month. choice What survives the crash is the trade: Japan now has a dozen nurseries that know how to grow, graft and ship Western roses, and a public that wants them (Part XII).

June. Tanabe (Miyake) Kaho publishes Warbler in the Grove, usually counted the first modern novel by a Japanese woman, a satire of the Westernised girls of the Rokumeikan years, written while she was still at school. documented In this timeline reviewers compare it, unfavourably, with Utena; Kaho's satire of a Westernised girl is read as an answer to the serial's girls, and the fee she earns will, a few years later, persuade Higuchi Natsu, the future Ichiyō, that a woman can live by writing, as in our history. documented for the fee's effect on Ichiyō; choice for the comparison.

10 July.
