Kobayashi Ichizō's girls' opera of 1914 was a device for filling the trains of his Minoo-Arima Electric Railway on the way to his hot-spring resort; the audience saw the show free with their bath, about 1,100 of them a day in the first season, and the girls, most with only an elementary education, were paid as much as university graduates. documented In this timeline the Takarazuka Utena of 1919 is the company's first full-house run of a new piece, and the railway's Sunday traffic to Takarazuka doubles in the year it opens. choice Over the century the revue's Utena plays to more people than any other piece in its repertoire, more than the Rose of Versailles, which in our history reached five million spectators in 2014. documented for the Rose of Versailles; choice for Utena.

A classic nobody owns

Most of Utena never had an owner. Under the press and copyright rules of the 1880s a newspaper serial could not be collected into a book for two years without the editor's consent, and was protected after that only if someone registered it; the Copyright Act of 1899 gave nothing to works that had been published unregistered under the old law, and protected an anonymous work for thirty years, counted from the year after publication. documented Pirate editions of popular serials were common: Sakazaki Shiran's life of Sakamoto Ryōma was pirated while it was still running in 1883. documented In this timeline the newspaper text of chapters 1–33 is pirated from the late 1880s, in booklets that print the circles of 1886 as faithfully as the words, and only Shun'yōdō's registered book editions of Part Four and the collected text are protected, until the end of 1917 and 1918. Shun'yōdō shares the rights with the Tokyo Asahi after a dispute in 1900–02, and from 1 January 1919 the whole book is free. choice The economic consequence is the opposite of what the book's publishers feared. A public-domain classic is a free raw material, and everybody uses it: eleven editions in two years, the cheapest of them ten-sen booklets at railway kiosks; films from 1918, using the unprotected newspaper text; the Takarazuka operetta; the one-yen sets of 1926–27, in which Kaizōsha's first set alone drew 230,000 subscribers at a yen a volume, about two per cent of a graduate's first month's pay. documented for Kaizōsha; choice for the rest. Every company that adapts the book adds to the audience for every other adaptation, and none of them owes the author a sen.

After the war the textbook editions make it one of the steadiest sellers in Japanese publishing (Part X), and the 1997 television series, which in our history earned its makers royalties on an original work, in this timeline earns them royalties on an adaptation of a free one, which is the business model of every adapter of Dickens and Austen. inference

The ledger

WhoWhat the book did for them
Jiyū no Tomoshibi and its successorsA larger sale for three years; a better price when sold to the Asahi in 1888 choice
Shun'yōdōThe protected book editions of 1887–88, shared with the Asahi until 1918; the one-yen set volume of 1927; the unclaimed author's fees choice
Lending librariesTheir most rented item, 1885–88 choice
Rose nurseries of Yokohama and KomagomeA boom, a crash, and then a lasting trade choice
Tailors, ring-makers, printers, photographersThe first schoolgirl market choice
The Misaki-za and the women's kabuki companiesA house piece for ten years choice
Kobayashi Ichizō's railway (later Hankyū)Its revue's biggest draw choice
The authorAbout thirty yen a month while the serial ran, April 1885 to October 1886, and nothing after choice

Shadow play · Part XII

ABlack roses! Thirty yen! Genuine, from the Black Rose Book!

BWhy is my black rose turning red?

ABecause it is growing up.

XIII

What did not change

The limits of a book, stated plainly

A novel can change what people take for granted, give a movement words and pictures, and tip a decision that was already close. It cannot stop a war, close a mill, or move votes that money and armies have already decided. Most of modern Japanese history runs the same way in this timeline as in ours, and the divergences only make sense against it.

The empire and its wars

Taiwan in 1895, Korea in 1910, Manchuria in 1931, China in 1937, Pearl Harbor in 1941, Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945: all happen as they did. documented for our history; inference that the serial changes none of them. The forces behind Japanese expansion were strategic, economic and ideological, and a girls' novel touches none of them. Its readers were, if anything, a little more likely than other people to oppose the wars, and a little more likely to be harassed for it. That is all. inference

The throne

The constitution of 1889, the Rescript on Education, the cult of the emperor in the schools, the lèse-majesté prosecutions: unchanged. The Imperial House Law of 1889 still restricts the succession to men; the serial's first effect on the law, as Part VI argued, was to give conservatives another reason to write it that way. inference The question returns only in 2005 (Part XI).

The mills and the quarters

The women who made Meiji Japan rich, the silk reelers and cotton spinners who were the majority of the country's factory workers, lived in this timeline as they did in ours: on contracts signed by their fathers, in locked dormitories, on working days of thirteen hours and more, up to seventeen or eighteen in the reeling mills of Suwa, as the government's own survey of 1903 recorded. documented (Part XVIII) Utena reached them late, read aloud, and as entertainment. The Factory Act of 1911 and its slow enforcement are the same. inference So is the end of licensed prostitution, abolished on paper in 1946–47 while the tolerated red-light districts lasted until 1958, in both timelines; the serial's world of girls' schools did not reach the brothel districts, and its readers' reformist energy went, as in our history, into the Christian temperance and purity societies. inference

The household

The Civil Code of 1898 is enacted in this timeline as in ours, and its household system governs Japanese families until 1947. What changes is one part of it, the wife's legal incapacity, abolished in 1931 instead of 1947 (Part IX), and the way the rest of it is talked about. The household head, primogeniture, the parents' veto on marriage until a man was thirty and a woman twenty-five, the double standard on adultery: all stay. inference

The political machine

The parties, the oligarchs and later the bureaucracy and the army decided Japan's politics, and in the post-war decades one party did. A cultural change moves votes at the margin, and in this timeline it moved enough for women's local suffrage, which the government itself had brought in, to pass the Peers in 1931. It does not move the Liberal Democratic Party's factions, its rural base or its money. In this timeline as in ours the LDP governs for most of the years after 1955; in both, Japan's first woman prime minister takes office only in 2025. choice That is the hardest of this document's convergences to defend, and it is defended in Part XI.

The canon around it

Most of the books, plays and pictures of our timeline exist in this one. Takekurabe, Seitō, Flower Tales, the Takarazuka Revue, Princess Knight, The Rose of Versailles: all are made, by the same people, at roughly the same time. choice The counterfactual convention followed here is that people born after 1885 are still born and still do their work, unless the serial gives them a strong reason to do something else. Strictly, a change in the past changes which children are born; following that rule would empty the twentieth century of everyone we know, which would make the history unreadable and teach nothing. This document keeps the people and lets the book act on them.

Utena itself

The strangest convergence is the one the premise makes inevitable. In 1997, in this timeline as in ours, TV Tokyo broadcasts a thirty-nine-episode animated Revolutionary Girl Utena from April to December. documented for our history; choice for this one. In ours it is an original work. In this one it is an adaptation of a Meiji classic, and the most faithful one ever made (Part XI).

XIV

Who was Hōsūshi?

The authorship question, as the scholars of this timeline argue it in 2026

Nobody knows who wrote Otome Kakumei Utena. A hundred and forty years of argument have produced a short list of serious candidates, one strong piece of internal evidence, and a consensus that the question cannot be closed.

The name on the page

The byline 鳳雛子 carried the newspaper's reading ほうすうし, Hōsūshi: "Master Fledgling Phoenix". 鳳雛 is the sobriquet of Pang Tong, the strategist of the Three Kingdoms paired with Zhuge Liang as "the Crouching Dragon and the Fledgling Phoenix", whom the novel kills young at a place called Fallen Phoenix Slope. documented Every reader of 1885 knew the story. So the pen name says, at the least, "a young talent who expects to fall", and it holds the academy's own phoenix (鳳, ōtori) and the creed's unhatched chick (雛). choice

The same three characters can be read another way. 鳳 alone is Ōtori, and 雛子 is the girl's name Hinako. Read as a name, the byline is Ōtori Hinako, a girl who shares a surname with the academy. A reader's letter pointed this out in the paper's correspondence column on 19 June 1885 (Part XVI, document 2), and the newspaper never replied. Whether the ruby ほうすうし was the author's or a compositor's guess is unknowable, since the fair copies burned in 1923 and the surviving drafts carry no byline. A literatus's sobriquet on the surface, a girl's name underneath: the byline does what Utena's jacket does, and generations of readers have taken that as a hint. choice

What the paper knew

Very little, by its own account. The fullest testimony is the memoir of the paper's serial editor in 1885, published in 1909, which says that the first three chapters arrived by post in February 1885 with an unsigned note asking that no inquiry be made; that later chapters came in batches of two or three, posted in Yokohama and Tokyo; that fees went by postal money order to a different payee each time, collected at Yokohama's main post office; and that he never met, saw or identified the author. choice Postal money orders had existed in Japan since 1875, so the method was available to anyone. inference The law allowed the arrangement. The press law of 1875 had required writers to sign with their real names and punished pen names; its replacement of 1883 required only the paper's proprietor, editor and printer to be named, made them answer for what it printed, and made the author liable as an accomplice if found. documented A pseudonymous serial was legal so long as an editor would stand behind it, and this one did. The memoirist was writing twenty-four years later and had reasons to enjoy the mystery. Nobody else at the paper left an account.

The manuscripts stayed in the newspaper's files as it passed from Jiyū no Tomoshibi to Tomoshibi to Mezamashi to the Tokyo Asahi, and they burned with most of that paper's Tokyo archive in the fire after the earthquake of 1 September 1923. choice Twenty-three leaves survive because the serial editor had taken them home: drafts of parts of chapters 7, 22 and 39, in a quick, practised hand with corrections in a second ink. They were sold in 1931 and are now in the Tsubouchi Memorial Theatre Museum at Waseda, a home whose irony every scholar of the question enjoys. choice

The evidence of the text

Whoever wrote it knew three worlds well. The first is Yokohama and the Bluff: the academy's harbour view, its Western buildings, the foreign words, the habits of a mission girls' school from inside (dormitory rules, the piano, the hierarchy of seniors), the phonograph and the lift, which the author describes like a reader of the Iwakura Mission's published record rather than someone who had ridden one. The second is the old high culture: the fairy tale's frame is Western, but the narrator's asides, the punning headings and the Sino-Japanese of the creed belong to someone schooled in Chinese classics and Edo comic fiction. The third is the politics of 1884–85: the creed reads like a People's Rights handbill, and the letters from End of the World arrive with the gravity of imperial rescripts. inference

The text is also in two minds about Christianity, which it knows well. Lucifer, Revelation and the "sting of death" are used with exactness, and so is the Buddhist image hidden in the heroine's name: utena is the calyx of a flower and also the lotus throne on which the saved are reborn in the Pure Land, where to share one lotus seat (一蓮托生) once meant to share one fate after death. documented for the Buddhist usage. The serial ends with that image held out and not settled: two hands on opposite sides of a coffin lid, and no word on whether they share a fate. inference

The three hands

The strongest single finding came in 1979, when two statisticians, Ōta Keiko and Hayashi Satoshi, ran the full text through a word-frequency study on a university mainframe. They found not one author but at least three. choice

HandChaptersCharacter of the writing
A, "the principal hand"1–5, 7, 9, 13–15, 22–23, 25–26, 30, 33–34, 37–39 (20 chapters)The creed, the castle, the coffins, the Black Rose and its fire, Akio's three chapters of reckoning, the ending. Long sentences, heavy Sino-Japanese, every chapter that carries the design.
B, "the comic hand"6, 8, 10, 16, 18, 24, 27, 31, 32 (9)Nanami's chapters: the kangaroo, the curry, the cowbell, the egg, the diary; then, surprisingly, the two chapters in which she searches the family register and is left with something she cannot say. Short sentences, puns, Edo comic diction.
C, "the melancholy hand"17, 20, 21, 28, 29, 35, 36 (7)Shiori, Wakaba, Keiko, Ruka, Juri's broken locket, Tōga's confession. The most attentive to what women do to each other.
D11, 12Tōga's victory and Utena in the dress.
E19Tatsuya, the good boy turned away.

The study has been replicated twice, in 1998 and 2017 (the second time with machine-learning methods), and the A/B/C division has held each time. Its implication is that Utena was a planned work written by a small circle under one designer, who decided what every chapter must do and gave some chapters to other writers. That is how the ending of chapter 30 can be in hand A while chapters 31 and 32 are in hand B without the story losing its thread. The circle is usually called the "Hōsū group" (鳳雛社). Whether it included the designer's friends, students, a married couple or a teacher and her pupils is the whole of the modern debate. choice

The five hands map exactly onto the five people credited with the anime's scripts: Yōji Enokido (A), Ryōta Yamaguchi (B), Ryōe Tsukimura (C), Kazuhiro Uemura (D) and Takuya Igarashi (E), with Kunihiko Ikuhara as the designer who parcelled out the work. The scholars of this timeline cannot know that.

The candidates

Kishida Toshiko (1864–1901) the "Shōen hypothesis"

A former tutor to the empress, the most famous woman speaker of the People's Rights movement from 1882, arrested after her Ōtsu speech on "daughters in boxes" in October 1883, and married in 1885 to the Liberal leader Nakajima Nobuyuki, who had governed Kanagawa prefecture in 1874–76. documented Her essay to her "sisters" had run in ten installments in this very paper in May 1884, and she had known Miyazaki Muryū since 1881. documented She was baptised with her husband in 1886, taught Japanese and Chinese studies at a Tokyo mission girls' school from 1887, followed him into exile in Yokohama after the expulsions of December 1887, and from May 1888 was an honorary professor at Ferris. documented She knew the court, the party, the paper, the Kanagawa coast and the girls' schools from inside. Against her: her known prose is stiffly classical and humourless, and hand B could not be hers; her supporters reply that hand A could be, and that the comic chapters were given to someone else. This is the leading hypothesis in surveys of Japanese literary scholars, and has been since the 1950s. choice

Wakamatsu Shizuko (1864–1896) the "Ferris hypothesis"

Born in Aizu in 1864, four years before its siege, raised in Yokohama, one of the first graduates of the mission school on the Bluff, in 1882, and a teacher there, a Christian who read English as easily as Japanese and who would later translate Little Lord Fauntleroy as Shōkōshi, the little young lord. documented She had the school, the language, the fairy tales and the Aizu dead (whom chapter 22 seems to remember). Against her: she was twenty in 1885 and published almost nothing before 1886, and her later style is plainer than hand A. Her supporters make her the designer and the youngest member of a circle. choice

Miyazaki Muryū (1855–1889) the "house writer" hypothesis

A Tosa journalist and the Liberal press's best writer of political fiction, who had adapted Dumas's French Revolution and written of the Russian nihilists and their women. documented His nihilist serial had just finished in this very paper, and its book was banned and he convicted while Utena was running. documented The hypothesis is that he wrote the next serial for the same paper and disguised himself to protect it, and the Kishida–Muryū "circle" is the commonest form of it, since the two had known each other since 1881. Against him: his known fiction has no comedy and no interest in girls as anything but martyrs, and he died in 1889 having never hinted at it. He is the favourite of political historians and nobody else. choice

Tōkai Sanshi (Shiba Shirō, 1853–1922) the "Aizu hypothesis"

An Aizu samurai's son whose mother and sisters died in the siege of 1868, back from Pennsylvania in January 1885, whose Chance Encounters with Beautiful Women began appearing that October and filled students' heads with beautiful women revolutionaries. documented The coincidence of year and subject made him a candidate in the 1890s. Against him: he was writing a very different book at the same time, in a very different style. The hypothesis survives mainly in combination: an Aizu circle (Shiba, Wakamatsu Shizuko and Ōyama Sutematsu) is a staple of popular histories. choice

Tsubouchi Shōyō (1859–1935) the "experiment" hypothesis

The young critic who was publishing The Essence of the Novel in parts from September 1885, arguing that fiction should depict human feeling as it is, and his own novel of student life under a pen name. documented The theory is that Utena was his experiment in feeling within fantasy, run anonymously so as not to compromise his critical position. Against him: his correspondence shows no trace of it, and his treatise never mentions it, though his followers judged it by his terms (Part V). That silence is, inevitably, offered as evidence for him. choice

Others

  • A former lady of the shogun's inner palace. The "Ōoku hypothesis" (first proposed in 1956): only someone who had lived in a closed world of women run by an absent man would write End of the World's letters so. No candidate has ever been named. choice
  • Ōyama Sutematsu or Tsuda Umeko, the American-educated women back from the Iwakura Mission in 1882. Both had largely lost their Japanese (Tsuda had left at six), which disposes of the theory and keeps it popular. documented for their language difficulties.
  • The illustrator (Part III), on the ground that he knew the paper and the story better than anyone; no more. choice
  • Higuchi Ichiyō, who was twelve. A modern novelist's conceit that every few years someone takes seriously. choice
  • The Empress Haruko, a 1960s pulp theory built on her poetry and her patronage of girls' schools. Nobody takes it seriously. choice

The cancelled ending

One leaf of the chapter 39 draft has been read, under infrared since 1988, as a cancelled ending in which it is Anthy who vanishes and Utena who walks out of the academy alone. A single line, struck through, ends with Utena at the gate and the gate closing behind her. choice If the reading is right, the author changed the story's end at the last stage, and chose the more surprising of two endings: the heroine disappears and the Rose Bride leaves. Scholars disagree about what this means for the authorship question. That the change happened at all is accepted.

This too has a twin outside this timeline. The anime's director said in 2003 that the opening credits show the ending as first planned, the two in armour, the castle falling, and Anthy disappearing, and that he reversed it in production because nobody would expect the heroine to vanish. documented (makers' statement, per the archive)

Where the question stands

A 2024 survey of 312 scholars of Meiji literature found 41 percent naming a circle with Kishida Toshiko at its centre, 22 percent a circle centred on Wakamatsu Shizuko, 9 percent Miyazaki Muryū, and 19 percent declining to name anyone. choice Most agree on three things: that more than one person wrote the text; that at least one of them was a woman who had been inside a girls' school; and that whoever designed it meant the byline to be read both ways.

XV

The text and its editions

Nine states of one book, and why no two readers born a generation apart have read the same Utena

Like many Meiji serials, Utena exists in several versions: a newspaper text, part-volumes, a book, a collected edition, censored and restored printings. Unlike most, its differences are about the things the story is about.

StateDateWhat it containsWhat is missing or changed
1. Newspaper text2 Apr 1885 – Oct 1886Chapters 1–33 in about 200 daily installments, each with one woodblock cutSelf-censored after the suspension of August 1886: two passages of chapter 32 and most of the inn scene of chapter 33 replaced with rows of circles; the last cut of chapter 33 printed as a blank frame captioned 此図差控, "this picture withheld"
2. Confiscated issueAug 1886The issue that drew the suspension, with the end of chapter 31 as writtenOrdered seized on the day of publication; about forty copies survive, most bought by collectors in the 1920s. The only printed source for the uncut end of chapter 31.
3. Part-volumesSept 1885, Apr 1886, Dec 1886Parts One to Three reissued as illustrated paper-covered volumes, three per part, with colour-printed covers in the old gōkan mannerFollow the newspaper text, including its circles
4. Part FourApr 1887Chapters 34–39, never serialized, as a typeset book with woodblock platesSubmitted to the Home Ministry as the law required; one passage of chapter 35 (the white horse) cut at the censor's request before release
5. Collected edition1888, four volumesAll 39 chapters, revised; the standard text for fifty-eight yearsJuri's surname printed 有須川 in place of 有栖川, the name of a living imperial prince's house, same sound, different characters; chapter 31's ending and chapter 33's inn scene shortened by the author or the publisher; the creed's "shell" kept everywhere, including chapter 15, where the newspaper had "cage"
6. School and "family" editions1893–1912Abridgements for younger readersParts Three and Four reduced to summary; Juri's locket holds "a friend's picture"; Akio's chapters cut to his courtship of Utena, which ends with a proposal
7. Pirated and public-domain editionslate 1880s; from 1919Pirated booklets of the unprotected newspaper text from the late 1880s; then, after the term on Shun'yōdō's registered editions ran out at the end of 1918, dozens of printings of the whole, from cheap paperbacks to the 1927 one-yen "complete works" setsThe pirates reprint the newspaper text, circles and all; the later editions mostly reprint the 1888 text, and a few restore chapter 31 from the confiscated issue
8. Censored title1937–1945Printings issued as 少女ウテナ, the word "revolution" removed even from the title, from December 1940 as ウテナ alone, then none at all in the last years of the war"Revolution" cut throughout without a mark, as the censors now required, and from 1940 "girl" in the title too; the creed's last line removed; chapter 34's mob of men in suits redrawn as foreigners
9. Restored text1946; critical edition 2002The 1888 text with the newspaper's readings restored where they are fuller, chapter 31 from the confiscated issue, 有栖川 back, and the withheld picture still blank, because no proof of it survivesChapter 33's inn scene exists only in the circled newspaper text and the shortened 1888 text; nobody has read what the author first wrote

Every row above is choice, built on documented practices: newspaper suspensions and seizures under the press law of the 1880s, the reissue of newspaper serials as illustrated paper-covered books, prior submission of books to the Home Ministry, and the blanking of words with circles or crosses (fuseji) in pre-war publishing. Part XVIII gives sources for the practices.

The blank frame

The withheld picture of chapter 33 is the most famous image in Japanese illustration that nobody has seen. The newspaper's practice when a cut was refused was to print the frame and a line of apology, and that is what readers got on the morning the inn scene ended: a ruled rectangle the size of every other day's picture with four characters in it. choice Over the next century the empty frame became a motif in its own right. It was printed on fans in the 1890s, drawn into girls' magazine covers in the 1920s, reproduced as a full-page blank in avant-garde magazines of the 1960s, and hung as an empty white panel in the 2016 retrospective at the Yokohama Museum of Art, where visitors queued to stand in front of it. choice In the anime's version of this scene the camera spends nearly two minutes looking straight down at Utena's face, and never shows the person she is talking to. The serial's empty frame does the same thing by another means.

The two names of Juri

Arisugawa was the name of one of the four princely houses of the imperial family. Its head in 1885, Prince Arisugawa Taruhito, had commanded the imperial army that marched on Edo in 1868, and had once been engaged to Princess Kazu, who was married to the shogun instead. documented To put that name on a girl who fences, loves another girl and keeps her picture in a locket was either very careless or very pointed. The newspaper text printed it without comment. When the collected edition went to the censors in 1888, the publisher changed one character: 有栖川 became 有須川, with the same sound. choice For fifty-eight years Juri was "Arisugawa" in every reader's mouth and something else on the page, and the substitution is itself a small classic of Meiji censorship: a name nobody could say had changed, and nobody could say had not. The Arisugawa house died out in July 1913 with Prince Takehito. documented The restored text of 1946 put the original characters back.

The two readings of the title

The newspaper glossed 少女 as をとめ, otome. Both readings of the characters were centuries old; in Meiji print otome was the poetic choice and shōjo the plain one, and the plain one became the usual gloss, and the name of a social type (the schoolgirl), only with the girls' magazines that began in 1902. documented Meiji readers said "Otome Kakumei". Their granddaughters, reading the 1920s paperbacks without ruby, said "Shōjo Kakumei". inference Older people in Japan still use the first reading, and saying "Otome Kakumei" now marks a speaker as either over eighty or a scholar. choice

XVI

Documents of the rose

Twelve period documents from this timeline, in English translation

Every document in this part is invented, and so is every person who signs one. The forms, places, institutions and dates around them are real, and each note says which real practice the document imitates. choice throughout.

Document 1 · 社告 · notice to readers

Jiyū no Tomoshibi, 1 April 1885

From tomorrow this paper begins a new serial story, Otome Kakumei Utena, by a contributor who has asked that his name, or hers, be left unasked. It concerns a school on a hill by the sea, a girl who wears a young man's coat, and a betrothal decided by the sword. Our readers know that this paper does not print idle tales. We print this one because it is not idle. Those who read it to their households may judge for themselves what it is about. Daily, with a picture.

Imitates the front-page notices with which small newspapers announced new serials. Unsigned; this timeline's historians attribute it to the paper's serial editor (Parts VI and XIV), who is invented. The paper's coy "his, or hers" is the first published hint that the author might be a woman.

Document 2 · 寄書 · readers' letters

Jiyū no Tomoshibi, 19 June 1885

To the editor. I am sixteen and attend a school on the Bluff, which I shall not name, where we read your paper in secret after lights out, one candle between six. We have noticed something your printers have not. Your author's name, read as you print it, is Hōsūshi. Read as a girl's name, 鳳雛子 is Ōtori Hinako, which is to say a daughter of the very academy in the story. We do not ask you to tell us who your author is. We only ask whether you knew. — A schoolgirl of Yokohama.

Imitates the readers' columns of the 1880s small papers, which printed letters, often pseudonymous, from students and, increasingly, from women. The paper did not answer.

Document 3 · 寄書 · readers' letters

Jiyū no Tomoshibi, 26 August 1885

Sir. My daughter is fourteen. Until the spring she called herself watakushi like a decent girl. Now she says boku and calls her brother kimi, and when her mother rebuked her she replied that there is no rule against it. I traced the phrase to your story. I do not ask you to stop printing it; my wife and her sister would not forgive me. I ask you to print, beneath the first installment when your story resumes, a line reminding girls that a novel is not a school. — A shopkeeper of Kanda.

Imitates complaints about schoolgirls adopting male students' speech (boku, kimi) and the new schoolgirl dialect, which were real and frequent in the press of the 1880s and 1890s.

Document 4 · handbill

A women's company at a Yokohama theatre, November 1885

Grand new piece in four acts, from the story everyone is reading: The Rose Bride of the Bluff. Iwai Tamaji's company of actresses, all parts played by women. Miss Tamaji as Tenjō Utena, in the coat; Miss Kogiku as the Bride. The duel in the forest garden with real swords and lanterns. The ball, with a Western orchestra. Doors at noon. Admission 6 sen, boxes extra. Ladies' gallery.

Imitates playbills of onna-shibai, the women's theatre companies that played in small houses in Meiji Tokyo and Yokohama. The company and actresses are invented.

Document 5 · official notice

Home Ministry, August 1886

Under the Newspaper Ordinance, publication of the newspaper Tomoshibi Shinbun is suspended from this day until further notice, the said paper having in its issue of the 21st instant printed matter injurious to public morals in the story entitled Otome Kakumei Utena, and having been warned. The issue of the 21st is to be seized wherever found.

Imitates the terse suspension orders published in the official gazette under the press laws of the 1880s.

Document 6 · the blank frame

Tomoshibi Shinbun, October 1886

[A ruled rectangle the size of the daily illustration, empty but for four characters:] 此図差控. [Below the installment:] To our readers. The picture for today is withheld. The story will be concluded in book form and will not continue in these pages. We thank the readers who have followed it for a year and a half, and especially those who wrote. The serial editor.

Imitates the practice of printing an empty frame or a line of apology where an illustration or passage had been withdrawn. Signed by the paper's serial editor, an invented person.

Document 7 · price list

A Western-plant nursery, Yamate, Yokohama, spring 1887

Roses, grown on our own grounds from French and English stock. Utena (white, scented, flowers repeatedly): one plant, 3 yen. Bride (deep red-violet, few thorns): 5 yen. Duellist (striped red and white): 2 yen 50 sen. Black Rose (deepest crimson, very rare; we have four plants): enquire. Orders by post. We regret that we cannot supply the green rose of the story, which does not exist.

Imitates the price lists of the Yokohama nurseries that sold Western plants to foreigners and to Japanese collectors. In 1885 a day labourer earned about 16 sen a day and a maidservant 75 sen a month, so "enquire" meant a great deal (Part XII).

Document 8 · from a dormitory rulebook

A girls' school in Tokyo, 1893

Article 11. Pupils shall not keep, lend or read in the dormitory the novel called Otome Kakumei, or any picture, verse, ring or flower relating to it. Article 12. Pupils shall not address one another as "Bride" or "Prince", nor exchange rings. Article 13. The forms of speech proper to young men shall not be used.

Imitates the dormitory regulations of Meiji girls' schools, which did ban particular reading and policed speech and friendships. The school is invented; Part VII discusses how common such rules became in this timeline.

Document 9 · review

A Paris weekly, 14 July 1900

Of the pieces Madame Sada Yacco plays at the Loïe Fuller theatre, the strangest is the fragment the programme calls La Fiancée des roses. A girl in a cadet's jacket fights a duel against a young lord over another girl, who stands between them in a crown and says nothing at all. The audience, which had come to watch a geisha die, did not know whether to laugh. Then the girl in the jacket won, held out her hand to the silent one, and the house rose. I have since learned that the original is a Japanese novel of 1885 called, if my informant is right, The Revolution of a Young Girl. Somebody should translate it.

Imitates Paris reviews of Kawakami Sadayakko's 1900 performances at Loïe Fuller's theatre at the Exposition Universelle, which drew writers and artists. The Utena fragment is this timeline's addition to her real repertoire.

Document 10 · letter

From a Chinese student in Tokyo to her sister in Shaoxing, 1906

You asked what the Japanese girls read. They read a book about a girl who becomes a prince in order to save another girl, and who fails, and they love her for failing. I have read it twice. Our teacher says it is a frivolous book. Then she lends it to us. When you come next spring bring your boots, because here we walk.

Imitates the letters of the Chinese women students who came to Tokyo in the 1900s, among them Qiu Jin. The writer is invented; Part VIII discusses how this timeline's critics read Qiu Jin's own verse-novel beside it.

Document 11 · censor's note

Home Ministry, Police Bureau, Book Section, 1937

Application to reprint: Shōjo Kakumei Utena (Meiji 21 text). Permitted on condition that the word "revolution" be removed throughout, including the title, without blanks or marks of omission; that the closing line of the so-called creed be deleted; that the illustration to chapter 34 not show the crowd in Western clothes as Japanese. Note for file: this is the eleventh application for this title since 1933. The book is not dangerous for what it says but for how many people know it.

Imitates the internal notes of pre-war censorship. Publishers had long blanked words such as "socialism" themselves to avoid bans, and from 1936–37 the Home Ministry suppressed the blanks too, because readers could guess what they hid; the order on this title is this timeline's.

Document 12 · examiner's sheet

Civil Censorship Detachment, Press, Pictorial and Broadcast Division, Tokyo, 1946

Title: Shōjo Kakumei Utena (restored text). Subject: novel, Meiji period, sword combat throughout. Recommendation: approve. Examiner's remarks: Sword fighting here is not feudal; the swords are drawn out of people's chests and the hero is a schoolgirl fighting the head of a household. The censored words restored in the title are "girl" and "revolution", which we are told were cut by the Japanese authorities in 1940 and 1937. Suggest no action. Suggest, in fact, that someone in G.S. read it.

Imitates the examiners' sheets of the Occupation's censorship, which did suppress "feudal" sword-fighting films and plays in 1945–49. G.S. is Government Section, which drafted the 1946 constitution.

XVII

The two timelines side by side

Where they part, where they meet again, and by how much

Most of the dates in this document are the same in both timelines. The serial does not move wars, cabinets or the throne. It moves a handful of things that concern women, girls and the people who love them, by a few years to a few decades, and almost always in the same direction. The chart shows ten of those milestones; the table after it runs through the whole period year by year.

Year by year

YearOur history documentedThis timeline
1885Jiyū no Tomoshibi, which had printed Kishida Toshiko's essay to her "sisters" in 1884, runs Miyazaki Muryū's nihilist serial until April; the Liberal Party has been dissolved since October 1884.The same paper begins Otome Kakumei Utena on 2 April. Schoolgirls on the Bluff adopt the black jacket.
1886The paper becomes Tomoshibi Shinbun. Cholera. The Tokyo Women's Reform Society is founded.The Black Rose and Carriage Books; the serial is suspended in August after chapter 31. The rose fever.
1887The empress's memorandum on Western dress; Itō's fancy-dress ball; the Peace Preservation Ordinance expels 570 activists from Tokyo.Part Four appears as a book. Akio is Itō in every reader's mind. Kabuki's first Utena.
1888The paper becomes the Tokyo Asahi. Matsuoka challenges Inukai to a duel; "the duel is the flower of civilisation".The collected edition. The rose bubble bursts. The papers call every challenger a duelist.
1889The constitution; the Imperial House Law closes the throne to women; the Duel Act.The same laws. The Duel Act is "the Utena law". A schoolgirls' duel on the Bluff.
1890Women barred from political meetings and parties; the Rescript on Education; the Ryōunkaku's lift.The same. The lift is "Utena's lift". A petition of former mission-school girls.
1893The Misaki-za becomes a home for women's kabuki under Ichikawa Kumehachi.Its first new piece is an all-woman Utena, Kumehachi as Akio.
1898The Civil Code's household system takes effect; wives are legally incapable.The same law; its articles on wives are "the Rose Bride articles".
1900–1912Girls' magazines; Sadayakko in Paris; Qiu Jin in Tokyo; Seitō; Nora on the Tokyo stage.The same, with the "Anthy story" in every girls' magazine, a fragment of Utena in Paris, a Chinese Utena in Tokyo, and Nora reviewed as "the Norwegian Anthy".
1914–1919Takarazuka's first show (1914); the first films made with actresses in place of female impersonators (released 1919).The same, plus a Takarazuka Utena (1919) and a filmed duel with women in every part (1918).
1919—The whole of Utena enters the public domain; its newspaper text has been pirated since the 1880s.
1921–1922The Peers reject (1921), then pass (1922), the amendment letting women attend political meetings.Passed at the first attempt, in 1921.
1931The Peers reject the government's bill for women's votes in local elections.The Peers pass it, without the husband's-consent clause; wives become legally capable.
1933The revue strike led by Mizunoe Takiko.The same strike; and women vote and stand in town and village elections.
1937–1945War; censorship; the women's movement absorbed into the state.The same war. The title is cut to Utena.
1946–1948Women vote (39 elected); the new constitution's Article 24; the household system abolished.Women vote again (57 elected); the same constitution and Civil Code.
1950sThe classics reissued in new spelling.Utena enters the high school textbooks.
1971Japan's first lesbian circle; Barazoku, and "rose" as slang for men's love.The same circle; the magazine is Yurizoku, because the rose already belongs to women.
1974Takarazuka's Rose of Versailles.The same, as the second great rose of Takarazuka.
1989The "Madonna boom"; Doi Takako: "The mountain has moved".The same words.
1997An original anime, Revolutionary Girl Utena.The same anime, as an adaptation of the Meiji classic, with cars.
2005–2006A panel recommends opening the throne to women; a prince is born; the bill is dropped.The same, with the 1886 argument turned round.
2015Shibuya's first partnership certificate, to a former Takarazuka male-role player.The same.
2021–2024Courts begin finding the marriage law unconstitutional (Sapporo District Court, March 2021); from March 2024 the high courts agree.The Supreme Court rules (2023); the Diet passes a partnership law (2024).
2025–2026Takaichi Sanae becomes the first woman prime minister; 68 women elected to the lower house; the Grand Bench has not yet ruled on marriage.The same prime minister; 104 women elected; partnership law in force, marriage still argued over.
2026The house law is revised: a princess keeps her status on marriage, adopted men of the male line may pass on the throne, and women still may not reign.The same law, passed more narrowly.

Read down the right-hand column and a pattern shows. The serial's effects cluster at three moments: the late 1880s, when it was news; the 1910s to the early 1930s, when the girls who had grown up on it were adults with votes to lobby for and stages to fill; and the present, when a century of being taught has changed what a majority thinks is normal. Between those moments the two timelines run almost together, and at every point where the state used force, in 1887, 1890, 1925, 1937 and 1940, they run exactly together. inference That is this document's argument about what a book can do, in one table.

XVIII

Sources and method

How the real history was checked, what could not be, and where to read further

Every statement tagged documented was checked against a source, nearly always one read in full during the research for this document. The sources below are the ones the argument leans on most; the working notes behind them cite about eleven hundred pages.

How the research was done

  • Fifteen research reports were compiled before and during the writing: on the Meiji press and serial fiction; press and book censorship and the laws on dress, swords and duels; the Rokumeikan and the schools; Meiji technology; women and the law; theatre, the women's stage and fandom; Meiji politics, ideology and the economy; the twentieth century from Seitō to 2026; the international reception routes; the vocabulary of 1885; and five independent checks, on the names of courts and schools, technology, education and dress, law and copyright, and culture and the arts. Each fact in them names the page it was read from. The finished text was then read by independent reviewers for errors about the show, the Meiji period, the modern period, its own consistency and the rules it sets itself.
  • Kinds of source. Japanese reference works as reproduced on Kotobank (Nihon Kokugo Daijiten, Nipponica, Sekai Daihyakka, the Yamakawa and Ōbunsha historical dictionaries); Japanese Wikipedia read as source text, used for dates and cross-checked where it matters; the National Diet Library's catalogue, reference database and exhibitions; statute texts from the Nagoya University historical statute database, Japanese Wikisource and e-Gov; the Ministry of Education's centennial history of the school system; the statistical yearbooks digitised by Hitotsubashi University; university repository papers; and memoirs on Aozora Bunko, above all the critic Okamoto Kidō's recollections of the Meiji stage.
  • The show was checked against a first-hand reference archive of Revolutionary Girl Utena (all 39 episodes watched shot by shot), which keeps what is on screen apart from what its makers said and what critics have argued. The makers' statements quoted in Part XI are attributed as such.
  • Limits. The research's search budget ran out before every question was settled, and some sites could not be reached. The points that stay open are listed below rather than smoothed over.

Still open

  • Whether any prefecture kept a ban on cross-dressing in its police rules after the national Penal Code dropped it in 1882.
  • Which rule barred women from the galleries of the lower house in 1890. The ban, and its lifting on 3 December after women wrote to the parties, are documented; the instrument itself was not found.
  • Whether a book whose author would not give a name could be registered at all, as Part VII assumes. The book ordinance of 1875 punished anonymous and pen-named books; whether naming a compiler in the colophon, as Part VII has Shun'yōdō do, would have satisfied the later ordinance was not established.
  • The circulation of Jiyū no Tomoshibi in numbers: the dictionaries say only that it was for a time the largest in Tokyo.
  • The vote by which the House of Peers rejected the women's civic-rights bill in 1931; a figure of 184 to 62 circulates but could not be traced to a primary source.
  • A single traced instance of 革命 printed as ××. The reference works name it among the words publishers blanked from the 1920s to the mid-1930s, but no particular page was found.
  • Whether Judith Gautier's 1885 Poèmes de la libellule were made from literal versions by Saionji Kinmochi, as is often said.

An alternate history written in October 2026. The serial, its author, its editions and everything marked choice are invented; everything marked documented is real and sourced in Part XVIII. Revolutionary Girl Utena (1997) belongs to Be-Papas, Chiho Saito, Shogakukan, Shokaku Iinkai and TV Tokyo; nothing from its songs is reproduced here, and nothing from its scripts beyond a few short lines of dialogue quoted in Parts IV and VI and a few words of its makers' published statements, attributed where they appear, and the Japanese lines from the imagined serial are new writing.
